#6239. The 8 Best Portable Power Stations for Outages and Outings

Be prepared for unexpected power failures and off-the-grid camping trips.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Portable power stations are handy for backup power during outages, off-grid electricity for an RV, or simply charging your laptop and phone while working remotely. They’re effectively large bundles of rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, which provide a quiet, exhaust-free alternative to noisy gas-powered portable generators.

Portable power stations come in a broad range of sizes from brands like Jackery and EcoFlow, including smaller models capable of charging a few devices and high-capacity backup units to keep your lighting and critical appliances on during a days-long blackout. Plus, most can be recharged using solar panels.

We evaluated eight power stations of varying sizes, focusing on each model’s maximum output, capacity, charging time, and portability. To test max output, we connected enough electronics and appliances to each power station to meet or slightly exceed its listed max output to see how well it could operate at maximum load. We then tested capacity, using an electricity usage monitor to record the total watt-hours each power station produced while running them under a consistent load.

Once they were drained, we charged each power station from 0 to 100 percent using its AC adapter, timing how long it took to get to 80 and 100 percent capacity. Finally, we evaluated each power station’s portability by attempting to carry it or roll it. Other factors that weighed into our decisions included the number and power output of each power station’s inputs and its charging options.

Our test team for this article includes David Dritsas, an editor who covers generators, lawn and garden, and more; Bradley Ford, an editor with more than five years of experience testing and writing about generators, generator maintenance, power tools, and lawn and garden equipment; and Tony Carrick, a frequent Popular Mechanics contributor who covers landscaping, home improvement, gardening, and home security.

Bluetti manages to pack a lot of power into the Elite 200 V2. It has a max output of 2,600 watts (with 3,900-watt startup power) and a 2,073.6-watt-hour capacity, all while being relatively compact.

We hooked up a miter saw, blender, and space heater, all three of which it powered simultaneously. It easily handled the spike to 4,000 watts to start up the saw, above its listed 3,900-watt starting power, before maintaining an even flow of around 2,500 watts.

The Elite 200 V2 also impressed with the quality of its battery. We recorded 92 percent of its listed 2,073.6-watt-hour capacity, well over the 85 percent average for most portable power stations. It has a quick recharge time for its capacity, going from 0 to 80 percent in 81 minutes and to full in just 107 minutes. And because it uses a LiFePO4 battery, it discharges and recharges for 6,000 cycles before it drops below 80 percent capacity.

The Elite 200 V2 gives you plenty of output and input options for its size, too. Four AC outlets allow you to load up multiple appliances. There are four USB ports for charging smaller devices, a car accessory outlet, and a DC output. Along with its power cord, there’s a port for charging from a car accessory port or with up to 1,000 watts of solar panels.

With a great power-to-weight ratio, the latest version of the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 is a great portable power station for powering a camper or providing backup power for the essentials.

A new and improved version of Jackery’s extremely popular Explorer 1000, the Explorer 1000 V2 features a slightly larger storage capacity, up 70 watt-hours, and a much higher 1,500-watt output—a 50 percent jump from 1,000 watts of the original. This allows you to power devices with higher loads, like an electric grill or a large microwave. Jackery managed this while maintaining the Explorer 1000’s compact size and weight, so it’s still easy to carry with you on a camping trip.

The Explorer 1000 V2 features three standard 120-volt AC outlets, two USB-C ports (30- and 100-watt), one USB-A port (18-watt), and one 12-volt DC outlet. Paired with Jackery’s app, you can monitor the power station locally via Bluetooth or from anywhere when it’s connected via WiFi. The app allows for checking charge levels and estimated run time, as well as toggling any of the outputs on or off. Plugged into the wall, the power station charges in under two hours. It’s also possible to charge it from your vehicle in up to 12 hours.

Performance-wise, the 1000 V2 did well powering a 25-cubic-foot refrigerator for 18 hours and 22 minutes, which is better performance than we’ve gotten from other tested 1000-watt models. Under a constant load of 475 watts (that’s a little less than a small coffee maker), it ran for 1 hour and 57 minutes.

This power station offers a lot of bang for the buck. Sure, it isn’t going to power your house through a days-long outage, but it offers a lot of nice features for the price, making it one of the better values out there, especially if you pick it up on sale.

What is most impressive about the Anker S2000 power station is its ability to maximize its runtime. During our testing, we were able to run a full-sized refrigerator for just over 24 hours, which is nearly six hours longer than other power stations we’ve tested with comparable capacity.

It does this using a technology that recognizes the type of device plugged in and adjusts the inverter's frequency to match the type of demand. This, in theory, helps reduce the amount of wasted power. From what we can tell, it works very well.

The S2000 is fairly well equipped, too, with five outlets for AC power (two are in the back) and a bank of USB ports for home use, and can operate as an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) for 10-millisecond automated backup. With only 1,500 watts of output, it may struggle with some high-power appliances like a large microwave, but for many people, this station can deliver power during a blackout and keep you up and running for a long time.

One of the standout features of Bluetti’s Apex 200 is a maximum solar input of up to 3,000 watts. You rarely find that much input power for a station of this size. There are two sets of DC inputs for this: low-voltage XT60 input (up to 1,000 watts) and high-voltage MC4 input (up to 2,000 watts). If you have the panels and enough perfect direct sunlight to achieve this full potential, you could fully charge this station in less than two hours using the sun’s rays.

Beyond that, the Apex 200 is a fairly robust power station, with 3,200 watts of continuous power. (It says 3,600 on the front, but that’s only if it’s connected to an expansion battery.) I ran my refrigerator for a full 27 hours on a single charge, and when I tested it for battery efficiency, I estimated it at about 90 percent, which is very good for a power station. There’s also a 120-volt 30-amp output if you wanted to run a few circuits in your home by hooking up to a manual transfer switch. Just keep in mind that there’s no 240-volt support, so you can’t use it to power high-voltage appliances like electric dryers.

The 2,560-watt-hour battery capacity isn't huge—at least not for home backup—but you can expand it by adding up to six additional batteries. That could add up to over 33 kilowatt-hours if you use the largest batteries Bluetti offers, the B500K. That’s massive.

Even with all this power, the Apex 200 is still a fairly portable station. Weighing 59 pounds, it’s not too hard to move around the house or in and out of a vehicle. So, when you’re not using it for home backup, it’s perfect for taking on a long outdoor trip or for powering an RV when a site hookup is not available.

Full Bluetti Apex 200 Power Station Review

This is one of the most rugged power stations we’ve seen yet. The Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra features an IP65 weatherproof rating, molded rubber port covers, a shockproof enclosure, and a bottom drainage system and cooling structure that help keep water out of the enclosure. All work together to resist the elements better than most power stations can.

The unique cooling system was particularly interesting. A titanium alloy plate within the structure helps dissipate heat without the need for multiple fans and eliminates the need for any side vents (typical in most power stations) that could allow droplets of water in. Meanwhile, you can remove an external plate on the bottom and dry it if water does make its way in.

The 1,800 watts of output power and 1,536 watt-hours of battery capacity are decent if you’re taking this camping for the weekend and need to recharge devices, run a low-powered small appliance or two, and plug in some lighting. But don’t expect to run something like a space heater for very long, though.

Full Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station Review

The S5000 is the second power station in Anker's S-series, which features inverter efficiency technology that helps to reduce wasted energy when the inverter is idling or running lower-powered devices. We were impressed with how this technology performed in the S2000, and this model matched that performance.

We ran this through several tests, and the battery efficiency proved to be around 97 percent (the industry average is around 89 percent). For example, we left the AC inverter idling for 18 hours, and the battery remained at 100 percent capacity. Meanwhile, another station we idled at the same time lost 19 percent of its available power. That was impressive.

The next most impressive attribute about the S5000 is its size. It’s at least half the size of other power stations that feature 5,000 watt-hours of capacity and includes just as many outputs, including a 240-volt, 30-amp outlet. It also has both high- and low-powered DC inputs that enable up to 3,000 watts of solar power input if you have the panels to generate that. You can also recharge at up to 4,500 watts using a direct DC connection to Anker's 5500 Smart Tri-Fuel generator.

With only 4,500 watts of total output, we wouldn’t call this a contender for true whole-home backup (Anker’s E-10 system is a better option for that), but the S5000 can deliver a decent amount to power an RV, run lights and appliances during an emergency, or even a couple of critical circuits.

During our hands-on test, Goal Zero’s newest Yeti 1500 impressed us with its capable performance and sturdy construction. It’s the replacement for an older model and improves on its predecessor with improved weatherproofing, more outputs, and a better battery.

This 2,000-watt power station is clearly designed for outdoor use with an IPX4 water-resistance rating and new outlet shields that cover the ports and inputs when you’re not using them. That’s great for dusty conditions. Each section is nicely illuminated by an LED light and can be individually turned on/off using a manual button or the mobile app (and will shut off if not used after a duration of time). These additions make it perfect for camping or other outdoor uses. You can’t leave it out in the rain, but getting a bit of water on it won’t be a concern.

We loved the increased number of outputs on the Yeti 1500. There are now four 120-volt AC outlets and six USB ports: four USB-C (two are high-powered) and two USB-A ports, plus four 12-volt connections (though two of those are proprietary for Goal Zero accessories and not all that useful in our estimation). There are also inputs for AC power, 12-volt DC, and inputs for both low- and high-voltage solar power that can be used simultaneously. Theoretically, you could recharge this station with up to 900 watts of eco-friendly electrical current.

As part of our test, we simulated a blackout at home and managed to run a cable modem/Wi-Fi router, a lamp, a TV, and a tower fan, while simultaneously charging a phone and a laptop through the USB-C ports. Given the station’s output and capacity, there was enough power for over two days of use (conveniently shown on the main display), and there was plenty of room to spare for a few more devices.

The mobile app was easy to use and chock-full of great information on energy consumption. The only problem we had was maintaining a stable Bluetooth connection. It needed to be manually paired every time we went to use it, which was annoying. Wi-Fi is available, but that’s not so useful when you are off-grid.

We should warn you that the Yeti 1500 is heavy at 53 pounds. If you’re taking it on a trip, you’ll need a bit of strength to lug it around. That aside, the 2026 Yeti 1500 is a well-designed power station that’s ideal for off-grid camping, especially when there are dusty or wet conditions. We’d happily take it on our next camping trip.

Though it’s no longer EcoFlow’s flagship backup power solution, the original Delta Pro is still a massive power station with a good amount of electrical output. The brand claims it powers nearly any appliance, and after testing, we’re inclined to agree. With an output of 3,600 watts, it can handle multiple appliances, and it’s possible to bump the output to 4,500 watts with its built-in X-Boost technology if you need more power.

In testing, we ran it with a continuous 470-watt load for 6 hours and 57 minutes, as indicated on the Delta Pro’s display. Of course, in a home backup during a power outage situation, we would run only the bare essentials to conserve power. To that end, we used it to power a full-size, 25-cubic-foot refrigerator, which it did for a remarkable 51 hours and 24 minutes.

Recharging the power station from empty using a standard 120-volt home outlet, it recharged to full capacity in 2 hours and 36 minutes. There’s also an included adapter for charging the system at EV charging stations, with solar panels (sold separately), with a car charger, or combinations of these to speed things up.

The Delta Pro’s display screen provides all the important information you need to manage your power consumption. We frequently checked the screen during testing to see the unit’s charge level, current load, and estimated run time at the current discharge rate.

All of this information is accessible through EcoFlow’s app, which was the most intuitive and easiest to use of those tested. We connected the app both locally using Bluetooth and remotely via WiFi to monitor the power station from anywhere. We could also toggle outlets on and off remotely, which is helpful if you’re trying to manage power station output to extend the battery life.

We’ve tested the brand’s Whole-Home Backup Kit, which includes two of the power stations and a dual-voltage hub used to connect to your home service panel via a transfer switch. We used this setup to power critical circuits in a Northeast Pennsylvania home in late winter.

The Delta Pro Whole Home Kit ran just over 24 hours, powering kitchen outlets, a full-size refrigerator, a chest freezer, a cable modem and wireless network, and a hot water boiler. Plus, having charged these two Delta Pro power stations previously, we found that they were able to hold a full charge for a full eight months.

Testing was performed under normal usage conditions—run time could easily be extended by employing standard power-conservation strategies like lowering the thermostat, powering the fridge and freezer for four hours on and four hours off, and only opening them when absolutely necessary.

EcoFlow’s Delta Pro Whole Home Kit is a legitimate home backup system that can operate inside your home, with none of the risks or potential hassles of running a generator, such as dangerous carbon monoxide gas from exhaust fumes and dealing with fuel and oil.

A portable power station’s maximum output tells you the total watts it can produce, which determines what you can and can’t power with it. Look for a power station that can handle the combined wattage of the electronics you plan to plug into it.

Some power stations also have surge power that allows them to produce higher wattage for short bursts. This is designed specifically for appliances that draw more watts (known as starting watts) in the first few seconds when you first start them up, including power tools, refrigerators, blenders, and window air conditioners.

A portable power station’s capacity, listed in watt-hours (Wh), determines how much energy a power station can deliver over time. Generally, power stations with more watt-hours can run for longer, but exactly how long depends on the amount of watts the devices connected to the power station draw. You can roughly estimate how long a power station will last by dividing the total watt-hours by the watts drawn (Wh ÷ W = Hrs).

For example, if you have a power station with 2,048-watt-hour capacity and are consistently drawing 400 watts of power: 2,048 ÷ 400 = 5.12 hours of runtime.

Keep in mind that the usable watt-hours are not the same as the watt-hours listed on the power station’s label. You’ll typically get about 85 percent of the listed watt-hours due to power lost in connections and the electricity that the power station itself uses to power its inverter and display. Given those losses, expect to get about 85 percent of a power station’s listed watt-hours in usable power. So, a fully charged 2,000-watt-hour power station will typically give you about 1,700 watt-hours of usable power.

These days, most portable power stations, including all those we recommend here, use LiFePO4 batteries, which are capable of holding far more cycles, which is the number of times a battery goes through a complete discharge and recharge, than older lithium-ion batteries, while also being less likely to combust. Their one drawback is that they have a lower energy density, which means it takes more LiFePO4 batteries than lithium-ion batteries to produce the same amount of power. Still, this is the battery type of choice for portable power stations, both large and small.

While all these power stations are portable, some are easier to transport than others. A power station’s portability is directly related to its power capacity and output.

Small power stations with around 300 watt-hours of capacity and a max output of 300 watts typically weigh under 10 pounds and are about the size of a lunch box.

Midsize models like the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 portable power station, which have a max wattage of between 2,000 and 2,600 watts and a 2,000-watt-hour capacity, are about the size of the printer in your home office and weigh around 60 pounds, just small and light enough for one person to carry from one room to another.

Large portable models can weigh up to 135 pounds and are about the size of a suitcase. While these monsters are too large for one person to lift, they do sit on wheels that allow you to move them over flat surfaces, technically making them portable.

Portable power stations have an array of output ports, including USB-C, USB-A, car accessory, AC, and RV. Consider what types of appliances or electronics you’re planning to charge and the type of connections they use when choosing a portable power station.

Since the wattage of the output can vary, also consider the maximum charging output of each port to avoid disappointing recharge times. For example, a power station with a USB-C port that has a 15-watt max output will take a much longer time to charge a laptop than one with a 140-watt USB-C port.

If you’re looking for a large-capacity power station that will back up critical circuits in your home or power an RV, you’ll need a station that features a single 30-amp connection that can connect to an RV input or transfer switch.

Portable power stations have control panels with LED displays and buttons that turn inputs off and on and display usage and remaining power. Most portable power stations are also compatible with Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, allowing you to monitor and control them remotely from a smartphone app.

Often, what makes a power station great is the kind of software it includes and what features it offers to help you best manage your power station. For example, some stations that you leave plugged into a wall—so that they stay charged and at the ready—will automatically only recharge your station during low-peak hours when rates may be lower from your electric utility. Features like this one can be incredibly helpful when trying to get the most from your station.

Most large power stations, including the EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus and Anker F3800 Plus, can serve as a UPS (uninterruptible power supply) for your home. To use these power stations as a UPS, plug them into the wall, then plug whatever devices you want backed up into the station’s AC output ports. When the power is on, those devices use energy from the grid. When there is a power outage, the power station instantly switches these devices to battery power. If you live in an area prone to power outages, this can be useful to prevent data loss from a connected computer, keep medical devices running, or run the pump and filter on a fish tank.

Portable power stations heat up when operating for extended periods or when they’re providing power for multiple devices. Internal fans will kick on to keep the power station from overheating. While these fans are far quieter than the roar of a gas-powered generator, they do still create some noise. Smaller power stations are about as loud as a small fan, while larger ones produce about the same amount of noise as a refrigerator.

A portable power station’s lifespan depends on the type of battery inside. Most new portable power stations, including all the models we recommend here, feature LiFePO4 battery technology, which lasts far longer than older lithium-ion technology.

How much more? LiFePO4 power stations will last for more than 3,000 charge cycles, or about 10 years. That’s far longer than the 500 or so charge cycles and 3 to 5 years you’ll get from an older power station with a lithium-ion battery.

That depends on the capacity of your portable power station, the wattage of your solar panels, and the weather. To figure that out, divide the station’s total capacity by the total input power of the solar panels (Wh ÷ W = Hrs).

For example, a 1,000-watt-hour power station that’s receiving a consistent stream of 200 watts of power from a solar panel would take about 5 hours to recharge. Keep in mind, this is assuming uninterrupted, direct sunlight conditions, which, even then, may produce varied results.

Some power stations have ingress protection (IP) ratings, indicating they have been tested for water and dust resistance. The Bluetti Elite 200, for example, has an IP65 rating, which means it can withstand water sprays from all angles. However, other portable power stations do not have a weather rating, so it’s important to check if you plan on using your power station outdoors. Regardless, it’s a good idea to protect your power station from any water or severe weather conditions as much as possible.

David is a Reviews Editor for Hearst’s Enthusiast Group, contributing to Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, Best Products, and Biography. He also spent years covering the ever-changing world of online retail. To relax, he loves experimenting with new recipes, tweaking his smart home setup, and spending time outdoors on his bike or camping.

Rachel is the Deputy Editor of Reviews for Hearst's Enthusiast and Wellness Group where she supports Popular Mechanics, Runner's World, and Best Products. Outside of work, Rachel can be found planning her next trip, visiting museums and galleries, and walking her wirehaired dachshund in Central Park.

#6238. As a Solo Traveler, I’ve Booked Tours Around the World—But This Fjord Excursion in New Zealand Took My Breath Away

After taking the 17-hour Air New Zealand flight from New York City to Auckland this May, I was determined to make the most of my first visit to New Zealand. I hopped around the North Island, relishing Auckland’s food scene, checking into the innovative Hotel Britomart, and visiting Wellington’s Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa. But when it came to the South Island, I realized the points of interest are far more spread out, with the massive Southern Alps to navigate through. The island has wide-open roads, but as an American conditioned to driving on the “wrong” side, I didn’t trust myself behind the wheel. So I turned to my favorite solution as a FOMO-fueled traveler who never wants to miss a highlight: scouring the GetYourGuide day-tour offerings to string together my ideal itinerary, a practice I’ve now participated in on all six continents.

I booked several day trips, from an Arthur’s Pass train tour starting in Christchurch to a Walter Peak farm tour in Queenstown. And while New Zealand’s natural beauty and the genuine Kiwi kindness made every experience enjoyable, the highlight was my grand finale: the Milford Sound Business Class small-group tour starting in Queenstown from a local operator called RealNZ. The round-trip 12-hour excursion brings guests in a glass-roof Mercedes Sprinter for stops along the iconic Milford Sound Road, then aboard a Milford Sound cruise through the fjord known as Piopiotahi in the Indigenous Māori language, which some consider to be the eighth wonder of the world.

The wide-open views from the Sprinter van

I was eager to see what “business class” would look like on a day trip, and the moment the doors to the Sprinter van opened, I was impressed. Each of the 14 black leather seats had a gray lambswool blanket, a plush green pillow, and a bottled shot of Manuka ginger Vitamin C boost juice. As a ginger shot addict who’s constantly searching for the best natural pick-me-up around the world, it was love at first sight.

The long journey ahead—five hours each way—immediately shrank as our amicable guide provided context about where we were, explaining Milford Sound’s history, ecosystems, and Indigenous Māori connections. When all was quiet in the car, there was Starlink Wi-Fi to keep travelers entertained by their screens. After a quick refresher stop an hour in at the rural settlement of Garston, we reached the lakeside town of Te Anau, where one of its downtown shops served as our business class lounge.

Here, the coffee order I’d requested at the top of the day was already waiting in a covered reusable mug with my name on it, alongside a plate of pastries. It wasn’t long before we entered Fiordland National Park, part of the UNESCO World Heritage site Te Wahipounam. I looked up through the translucent roof as foliage from both sides of the road enveloped our van, winding through the gentle curves.

Emerging through the Homer Tunnel, the writer stopped for this first glance of Milford Sound.

Soon, the narrow road opened up, and we made our first stop at Eglinton Valley, an expansive glacier-carved flat where expansive fields of golden tussock grass are broken only by striking triangular peaks. Not long after were the aptly named Mirror Lakes, where the Earl Mountains are reflected near-perfectly in the glassy, still water; and Falls Creek, a craggy cascade that unfolds into a teal pond. During our stop at Monkey Creek, we spotted a couple of kea, the world’s only alpine parrots known for their playful behavior. Next, we drove through the Homer Tunnel, traveling less than a mile through the solid rock of Darran Mountain. Fittingly, our guide changed the soundtrack to the Jurassic Park theme as we dramatically emerged into Milford Sound at last.

As we descended through the twisty road into the Cleddau Valley, there were gasp-worthy sights at every turn. One minute we were heading toward a daunting granite mountain wall and the next we were looking out to the waters of the sound in the distance. After a quick stop at a bridge to catch a glimpse of Fiordland's highest peak, Mount Tūtuko, in the distance, we arrived at Milford Sound Visitor Terminal to board the MV Sinbad.

A bridge across the Tūtoko River, which led to a view of Mount Tūtoko

The Cleddau Valley, with Milford Sound in the distance

That's when the premium service was cranked up a notch. After I was welcomed with a glass of local Cloudy Bay wine, I was led to my own bean-shaped wooden table with two cushy swivel chairs on one side and a couch on the other, set against expansive windows that stretched overhead for views of the peaks and falls.

A trio of dishes containing local ingredients, curated by chef Tom Hishon

Then came the five-course tasting menu. Already waiting was a seeded sourdough bun with whipped kelp butter, and it was followed by Fiordland wapiti (a local deer) bone broth soup. Next was a trio of artfully plated bite-sized dishes: paua (sea snail) with black garlic, a bite-sized fried ball made of titi (a local seabird), and roe from Mount Cook salmon. The penultimate dish was wapiti (elk) tartare with potato crisps plus smoked eel. It was all capped off with a “flat white”—an ice cream–topped dessert playing off the popular coffee drink.

Between dishes, the captain of the MV Sinbad talked us through the highlights of Milford Sound, steering us up close to its plentiful cascades, including Sutherland Falls (1,904 feet tall), Lady Bowen Falls (531 feet), and Stirling Falls (508 feet). When he noted that Niagara Falls is only about 180 feet tall, I thought I misheard and went over to ask. But despite the massiveness of Milford Sound, the falls exuded a calmness that overshadowed their height.

The area is home to bottlenose dolphins, Fiordland crested penguins, and humpback whales, and we caught a glimpse of a New Zealand fur seal lounging at Seal Rock. Throughout the two-hour cruise, the peaks—some craggy and pointy, others smooth and sloping—were a reassuring constant.

Feeling rejuvenated thanks to both the power of Mother Nature’s beauty and the gourmet dining, we eventually returned to the van, where a generously sized bag of Marlborough Sea Salt Proper Crisps was waiting on my seat along with a Whittaker’s bar, New Zealand’s most famous chocolate. Of course, since it is business class, I also received a refreshing hand towel as I boarded.

As we began the journey back to Queenstown, I gazed upward, soaking in the view from the car’s glass roof, with a contented smile. A rest stop later, I was so relaxed that I drifted off into a deep sleep. The next thing I knew, we were back in the city. We had spent 10 hours out of the 12-hour trip inside the van, but I hardly realized it thanks to all the luxurious touches at every turn. In this case, the journey was absolutely part of the destination.

The Milford Sound Business Class tour launched in October 2025 as a joint operation between RealNZ and Altitude Tours. I originally saw the offering on GetYourGuide, my preferred tour booking platform for its flexible cancellation policies, but you can also book directly through the RealNZ website. The excursion starts at $383 per person for the business class tour, but a coach version is also available.

The tour I took transferred from Queenstown, but RealNZ also offers the trip from Te Anau, as well as a self-drive experience. There’s also the option to book travel back to Queensland via a 45-minute flight in a fixed-wing aircraft for an additional cost, though it’s weather-dependent. For those seeking deeper immersion, there’s also an overnight cruise through Milford Sound, with the choice of private cabins with en suite bathrooms or shared bunk-style compartments.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

A spectacular sea of fog, a perfectly formed rainbow and dramatic lightning strikes feature among this year's winning photographs for Weather Photographer of the Year 2026.

The first light of dawn illuminates a sea of fog spilling over the rugged cliffs of Mallorca, Spain, in this year's winning Weather Photographer of the Year 2026 image. Photographer Francisco Bailón Rodríguez captured the scene from the Albercutz Watchtower, looking toward the Formentor Peninsula, after several days of high pressure and humid nights created the perfect conditions for fog to blanket the landscape.

On Nov. 17, the photograph, titled "Mares de Niebla (Seas of Fog)," was named overall winner of the Royal Meteorological Society's competition, which attracted more than 5,500 entries from photographers around the world.

The competition celebrates the ephemeral scenes created by weather, which can for brief moments transform landscapes into something extraordinary. Take a look at this year's winning photographs below and let us know your favorites in the comments.

Photographer Weilu Chen took second place in the main category with this spectacular image of golden light shining over the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge that runs for 34 miles (55 kilometers) across the Pearl River estuary in southern China.

A striking bolt of lightning illuminates a horizontal cloud during a thunderstorm, earning third place in the main category. These clouds are called arcus clouds that have a distinct shelf-like shape. "Mother Nature was kind enough to give us a supercell and lightning at night," photographer Laura Hedien said in a statement.

Photographer Mahmudul Hasan won first place in the public vote category for this image of the rolling tea hills of Long Coc, Vietnam, emerging through layers of mist.

Watching from Bayonne, New Jersey, photographer Dan Martland captured this triple lightning strike above New York City, earning second place in the public vote category.

#6236. The 7 Best Fireproof Home Safes Protect Your Valuables from Extreme Heat

Your standard safe may stop burglars, but can it also withstand fires and floods?

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

A good home safe will protect your most important items from theft and damage, but if you want one that will also offer protection from heat, direct flames, and even water (in some cases), you need a fireproof home safe. This protection isn’t just limited to non-flammable items like jewelry or firearms, either. High-quality fireproof safes keep cash, important documents, photographs, and passports safe, too.

To go one step further, home safes rated as fireproof will protect your belongings from house fires and sprinkler systems, but if you're looking for protection from natural disasters, there are solutions out there. A safe rated for extreme temperatures will safeguard your things in the event of a wildfire, and those with airtight seals should prevent water from seeping in even during a flash flood.

We’ve reviewed the best fireproof home safes below with picks that cover your needs regardless of what you’re storing or how much space you need.

We made our choices on this list based on extensive research, looking closely at key features, brand reputation, and of course, each model’s temperature and fireproof rating. We also looked through customer reviews, making note of how well their safes held up in real-world situations. Beyond this, we took into account recommendations from professional firefighters. Because of these factors, you won’t see a wide variety of brands on this list.

In previous versions of this article, we featured fire safes and chests that were tested out by our team. While these models have since been discontinued or are out of stock, we used this experience to inform new choices for this list. All the safes on this list are “true” fireproof options, meaning that the safe itself will hold up, not just an included fireproof envelope. Each safe we selected is rated to withstand temperatures of at least 1,200 degrees Fahrenheit.

More to Explore: Best Outdoor Security Cameras • Best Video Doorbell Cameras • Best Carbon Monoxide Detectors • Best Smart Locks

As you’ll see throughout this list, we believe in SentrySafe as a top brand for fireproof safes—for its lifetime warranty, $50,000 fire protection guarantee, and reliably high levels of fire protection across all products. This mid-sized, 1.23-cubic-foot option is the perfect choice for most people.

Alongside a fire rating of up to 1,700 degrees F for a full hour, the safe boasts a fully waterproof design that protects internal items completely for up to 24 hours in up to 8 inches of submerged water.

Beyond the powerful protection it offers, the fireproof safe also has internal organization features like key hooks, a shelf, and a lockable drawer for especially valuable items. The interior of the safe is even lit to help you see inside. That said, both the lights and the digital keypad are battery-operated, so you'll need to periodically replace them.

The safe, as a whole, weighs close to 90 pounds. While this is a great deterrent from a thief trying to simply steal the entire safe, it can make it quite difficult install or carry up stairs on your own.

As an affordable yet durable alternative to some of the higher-end models on our list, this safe from Amazon Basics checks a lot of our boxes. At 1.24 cubic feet, it's actually slightly larger than our Best Overall choice from SentrySafe, leaving you with just as much space inside, including a top shelf for organization.

The safe also comes with a digital keyboard for easy access. If the keyboard is damaged during a fire, the safe also comes with a backup emergency key that unlocks the mechanism manually.

The biggest detractor for this safe is its durability. The safe is only rated to handle up to 1,200 F for 20 minutes. This is considerably lower than many other safes on this list both in temperature and duration.

If you require more space and organization than our previous recommendations, this safe provides plenty. With over 2 cubic feet of space, there is significantly more room to store larger valuables, such as photo albums or antiques.

Furthermore, the internal organization boasts a top tray and a large bottom drawer, as well as key hooks and a small storage cubby on the door. Unlike other models on this list, the safe uses a dial lock which doesn't require batteries, but it can be cumbersome to use.

Like all SentrySafe models, this one will protect your items for up to an hour at 1,700 F and prevent moisture damage for 24 hours in 8 inches of water. This impressive durability extends to the outer strength of the safe, as well, which can handle a fall from 15 feet without significant damage. Because of its size and strength, the safe weighs a hefty 125 pounds.

Unlike the more traditional safes we recommend, this option from SentrySafe functions more like a secure file cabinet than a traditional safe. The chest holds up to 40 hanging files for easy document organization and has a small space on the lid for handheld items like passports or electronics.

While the safe gives up some fire protection compared to the classic options on our list (it’s rated for 30 minutes at 1,550 degrees), it more than makes up for this with its robust water protection. The file storage box can be fully submerged in water for up to 72 hours without the items inside seeing any water damage at all.

At 39 pounds, this safe is slightly more portable than the bulkier home options, though it is still relatively cumbersome to transport given the lack of handles or wheels.

This Sanctuary model stands out as the gold standard for fire protection. It’s capable of withstanding a blistering 1,800 F for 90 minutes. That makes it the best home safe to protect your valuables from the extreme heat of wildfires.

Additionally, with ETL-rated waterproofing, it can hold out for 7 days in up to 6 inches of standing water. The company also provides a lifetime warranty against fire, natural flood, and theft.

The LED-lit interior has two upholstered shelves and is California DOJ-certified for firearm storage. For security, the electronic lock has a timed lockout mode and tamper indicator. You can also enable an optional silent entry mode for added discretion.

Once you get this compact safe situated, at over 62 pounds, it’s not likely you’ll want to move it again. But, its sturdiness and heavy-duty construction are worth the extra money.

If you only need to protect a few small items, like your passport, a USB drive, and some jewelry, there’s no need to invest in such a large safe. This lock box safe from SentrySafe is small enough to be hidden away on a shelf in your closet, but it doesn’t sacrifice fire protection in the name of being compact.

Rated to handle up to 1,550 degrees F for up to 30 minutes, the lock box should be able to withstand house fires without much issue. The carrying handle also makes it easy to take this safe with you if you are evacuating the fire quickly.

Of course, because of its small size, there’s no internal organization. Everything just sits in the same compartment. But it’s not a feature-less safe. If you are interested in additional theft prevention, it comes with a bolt-down kit for securing the safe to your floor.

For security beyond just the physical integrity of the safe, the Mycube offers a biometric fingerprint scanner as the primary way to unlock its door. The safe saves up to 10 unique fingerprint IDs, so you can program it to open for you and your immediate family with ease.

If someone else needs access to the safe, you can also program a backup password they’ll enter from the digital keypad. Internally, the safe has a removable drawer for storing documents, small valuables, and watches. This also leaves the main compartment of the safe open for larger items.

The Mycube fire safe is quite durable with the company claiming it is capable of withstanding 1,700 F for up to an hour. Its worth noting that Mysafe does not use UL for its fire rating, though the company does report that the rating it has would be the equivalent of one from UL.

To withstand high temperatures, choose a safe that is completely fireproof rather than a security safe with a fire-resistant envelope. Unless all of your valuables fit comfortably in a fire-resistant envelope, the risk of damage to other items in the safe is far too high. Even in the envelope, your items will not be protected to the same degree as a completely fireproof safe.

For advanced protection, fireproof safes should withstand temperatures of at least 1,150 F for 30 minutes or more. In the case of wildfire risk, a fireproof safe that protects at temperatures up to 1,800 F is your best protection. Keep in mind, though, that wildfires get as hot as 2,000 degrees, which would melt most of the safes included here. Any safe you purchase should have fireproof ratings certified by either the Underwriter’s Laboratory (UL) or the inspection firm Intertek, designated by an “ETL” mark.

There are several different types of locking mechanisms available depending on the level of security you desire. Among our recommendations, you’ll find models with traditional keys, combination locks, and electronic keypads. Some safes also come with biometric locks that only unlock to your specific fingerprint, which may offer an additional layer of security.

The size of the valuables you need to store and the available space in your home will dictate the ideal dimensions for your fireproof safe. Look for a deeper safe if you need to protect a large cache of valuables or a variety of different-sized items.

Some smaller safes, like the Honeywell Small Safe Box Chest, are shaped like briefcases and work best for holding important documents. Similarly, if you are looking to store jewelry, look for deeper safes equipped with drawers or trays to better organize your items.

For a fireproof safe you can transport, look for a fireproof chest or document box that weighs 30 pounds or less. These safes are also light enough to be placed on a shelf. Heavier fireproof home security safes (upwards of 75 pounds and designed to deter thieves) usually specify and provide hardware for floor mounting.

Many fireproof safes that are water-resistant or waterproof may only be so under certain conditions, such as standing water of 5 to 8 inches, and possibly for only a certain duration of time. This ensures added protection of the safe’s contents when sprinklers go off in an apartment complex, or if the safe is in the direct line of heavy-duty hoses. Some fireproof security boxes or chests offer waterproof ratings anywhere from 8 to 72 hours spent submerged, which are optimal for homeowners who may face flood risks.

Fireproof rating is easily the most important feature to consider. An independent testing agency must rate the safe, and it should be able to withstand temperatures of at least 1,200 F. However, we recommend much higher for those who are worried about wildfires.

Beware of home security safes that companies list as fireproof, but aren't rated by a testing agency. Many of these safes do not have fireproof bodies and instead just include a small fire-resistant envelope to store sensitive items in.

Once the temperature on the safe interior gets above 350 F, any paper inside (including all your hard-earned cash) is at risk of scorching. Even rooms in a burning house that aren’t on fire can get above 600 degrees F at eye level, which is definitely hot enough to soften steel.

There are many things you can and should keep in a fireproof safe, but if it you need to keep the items chilled or temperature controlled, it shouldn’t go in the safe long term. Avoid storing volatile chemicals or batteries in a safe as they can deteriorate or spill and damage other valuables.

You might assume most safes are lock it and forget it, but they do require some maintenance. You should “air out” your safe to avoid moisture build-up every few weeks to a few months depending on the climate where you live and the contents of your safe. You should also replace the batteries in battery-powered safe locks once a year.

Avoid installing a safe in the master bedroom, where security experts indicate thieves are most likely to check for valuables first. Fireproof safes are heavy, so it’s preferable to store them on the floor even though it might make it harder for you to access.

In fact, large standing safes often have mounting hardware included so you can bolt them into the floor of your basement or garage for additional security and stability.

#6235. Solo meerkats can find their way back home

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Meerkats live, forage and raise their young in large groups. But they’ve still got solo skills

To test meerkats’ solo navigating skills, researchers outfitted the animals with GPS trackers, separated them from their packs, and followed their journeys back home.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

It was a hot, dry day in the Kalahari Desert, and Mathilde Martin was running after a meerkat.

The animal wore a GPS tracker around its neck and bolted between shelters, like an action hero running for cover, says Martin, a biologist at the University of Zurich. She and her colleagues had captured the meerkat earlier that morning, driven it 1.5 kilometers from its pack and then released it into the desert. They were trying to find out how well individual meerkats could find their way back home.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The answer was quite well, the researchers reported November 19 in the Journal of Experimental Biology. The results suggest that meerkats can navigate expertly on their own, perhaps relying on mental maps charted early in life. “They all seem to be very, very good,” Martin says. It’s a surprise finding for a species known for its group cooperation.

Meerkats (Suricata suricatta), which live in southern Africa, form tight-knit family groups of up to 50 members. These social animals cooperate in many aspects of life, including by babysitting each other’s pups and watching for predators while traveling along foraging paths. Martin and her colleagues thought meerkats might also rely on one another for navigating. Some pack members, perhaps those who’ve had more opportunity to explore solo, might have spatial knowledge of their territory and lead the rest, she says. But that’s not what the team discovered.

In separate catch and release experiments with 20 individual meerkats, 18 made a beeline back home, back to their group or back to the site where they were captured. (The other two may have been too stressed to get moving, Martin says.)

Neither age nor individual experience, which researchers had been tracking, seemed to factor into the meerkats’ homing skills. Nearly all of them knew where to go, Martin says. She thinks these crackerjack navigators relied on visual cues to orient themselves. They’d pop up on their hind legs and scan the landscape before scampering off in a direct line to their target.

It’s likely that scent played a role, too, though distant scent marks may have faded by the time the meerkats were released. The researchers dropped the animals off in territory they hadn’t visited for at least 30 days. “Otherwise,” she says, “it would have been a bit too easy for them to find their way back,” she says.

The best tote bags hold everything from our laptops, headphones, and water bottles to sleep masks and our most-used beauty products. #6232. The 8 Best Vacuums for Every Floor Type

I tried upright, cordless, canister, and robot vacs to find models that deliver reliable performance.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

When it comes to keeping your house clean, a reliable vacuum is a must. Vacuums are the quickest and easiest way to tackle dust bunnies, stubborn pet hair, and debris that collect in hidden corners. But not just any vacuum will do.

Finding the right vacuum is often overwhelming when you’re faced with sifting through dozens of upright models, robot vacuums, and more. A vacuum is a big investment, and an uninformed purchase often leads to disappointment if your choice turns out to be too heavy, too cumbersome, or not powerful enough. Plus, you want to pay for features you need without overspending on extras you’ll never use.

In this guide, we considered upright, cordless, canister, and robotic options from trusted brands, and evaluated them based on research and rigorous testing. We broke down key factors related to functionality, features, and maintenance to help you find the best vacuum, whether you need a pet-friendly option, one that’s powerful enough to clean up after kids, or a budget-friendly model.

More Home Appliances: Best Vacuums for Hardwood Floors • Best Dryers • Best Clothes Steamers

To find the best vacuums for every home, we first gathered a lineup of models across a range of brands, price points, and features. We deliberately chose a mix of canister, upright, stick, and robot vacuums to help ensure our selections accommodate different living situations, flooring types, and cleaning needs.

We focused on criteria like performance, ease of use, and versatility. For meaningful results, we ran each vacuum through a series of real-world tests to simulate common messes they’d be likely to come across in everyday life. We tried them on multiple surfaces like low-pile carpet, thick shag rugs, hardwood flooring, and bare concrete, seeing how well the vacuum adjusted to different demands. This also helped us assess suction power and how well the brush roll adapted to each surface type.

For debris, we chose materials that mimic typical household spills, like crumbled potato chips, popcorn, coffee, and cereal. The different weights and sizes of rubbish gave us a realistic view of how effectively the vacuum could remove the mess.

We also conducted similar tests with the handheld portions and attachments of these vacuums, using crevice tools and motorized brushes on couch cushions, on upholstery, and in tight corners. We noted how easy the tools were to maneuver, and whether they still packed enough power even when detached from the main unit.

By running each vacuum through comprehensive tests, we were able to get a clear picture of their real-world performance, so we could find dependable models for everyday cleaning.

I love using an upright vacuum for heavy-duty cleaning, and the AZ2002 packs the punch you need for tackling messes on carpets, couches, and floors. This model has two brushes: a soft roller brush and a foam-paddled brush. These work in tandem to increase contact with flooring and rugs, and I think that gives the vacuum a significant boost compared to models with just one traditional brush roll. The AZ2002 successfully picked up cat litter, dirt, and crumbs on a textured area rug.

All the cleaning modes are accessible right on the handle, so I was able to swiftly transition between carpet and laminate flooring without having to stop my cleaning session. The LED headlights brought attention to any dirt and gunk I missed during my initial swipes, too.

The AZ2002 also easily converts from an upright to a motorized canister vacuum. I especially liked using this functionality with the powered pet brush for cleaning couch cushions, so I didn’t have to haul the entire vacuum around. The hose and stick attachments extend to clean crevices and curtains, which I normally wouldn’t be able to reach.

The vacuum is on the heavier side, weighing a little over 16 pounds, but because it functions as a canister vac, I'm not too upset about sacrificing a little portability.

Full Shark AZ2002 Vertex Powered Lift-Away Upright Vacuum Review

I’ve had this vacuum from Shark for six years, and it has proved to be a reliable choice for apartments with hardwood, tile, area rugs, and two cats—so plenty of hair, litter, and dirt to go around.

I appreciate the Rocket for its lightweight build, convenient features, and usability. It transitions between hardwood and carpets using a switch right above the handle, and the base also detaches to become a handheld vacuum. The dustbin capacity is small, but that’s not uncommon for a stick vacuum. I just empty the dustbin whenever it gets too full by using the quick-release button.

The Rocket is easy to move around and underneath furniture, and it comes with useful attachments like a crevice tool, upholstery tool, and anti-allergen dusting brush for sucking up fine particles. The only bump in the road I’ve come across over the years is when I had a really shaggy carpet—the brush roll would often stop rotating and I’d have to untangle any fibers that got stuck.

You don’t get a ton of new tech with the Rocket, but I’ve found that it performs well on multiple surfaces. It also stores easily, and doesn’t require any hands-on effort emptying a bag or figuring out how to pair the appliance with a compatible app.

Full Shark HV301 Rocket Ultra-Light Corded Stick Vacuum Review

The Bissell Pet Hair Eraser has a tangle-free brush roll, and even after using the vacuum on two large area rugs and hardwood floors, I didn’t find any hair wrapped in the bristles. What I did find, however, was plenty of pet hair, dirt, and dander in the dustbin because the suction power is strong enough to agitate carpet fibers and pick up debris that might not be completely visible.

I use the Bissell Pet Hair Eraser Hand Vacuum on an everyday basis, so I was excited to see that this upright model comes with a dedicated pet hair attachment for the hose wand. I tried it on my couch cushions, and a couple of pushes back and forth removed a majority of the mess. Plus, the canister detaches from the base so you can carry it around as you clean.

The vacuum only has two settings, plush carpet and low carpet/bare floor, so it isn't as versatile as other vacs for different floor types. But I liked being able to manually turn the brush roll on and off with a control switch on the base, which helped me tackle different cleaning tasks.

When I think of canister vacuums, Miele comes to mind, and I’m willing to bet I’m not the only one. The brand is known for its powerful, well-designed canister vacuums, and the Classic C1 Turbo Team is, well, a classic.

It has six suction power settings, including options for hard floors, rugs, and even furniture. The floor head has a toggle switch that you can operate with your foot, switching between cleaning carpeting and hard floors easily.

The hose is long, which I found helpful because I didn’t have to lug the entire vacuum around as I cleaned. The cord is retractable, and the hose is completely detachable, so the C1 stores easily in a closet or laundry room. There’s also a removable component that holds the crevice tool and brushes.

The suction was impressive on low-pile carpets, but we wouldn’t suggest using this model on dense, thick carpets. The floor head also often lost suction during our tests. I particularly liked using this vacuum on furniture—it glided across the seat cushions, and the attachments came in handy for cleaning in between cracks and seams.

This style of vacuum captures dirt and other messes in self-sealing dust bags, so you’ll be able to clean for longer before needing to do any maintenance.

Full Miele Classic C1 Turbo Team Bagged Canister Vacuum Review

It might seem like cleaning is my favorite thing to do, given how many vacuums I’m testing regularly, but even I need a bit of a break sometimes. The Roborock Qrevo Series QV 35A has automated the process for me, so my weekly deep cleans don’t take nearly as long.

I have an 850-square-foot apartment, and it took about 30 minutes for the vacuum to map out my entire home. It worked its way over thresholds, across varied floor types, and in tight spaces with ease. I was impressed by how well it differentiated between carpet and hard flooring, so I didn’t have to worry about my area rugs getting wet during the mopping cycle.

It took 61 minutes for the QV 35A to vacuum my entire apartment. It worked around the perimeter first, and then moved in a zigzag pattern around the rest of the interior. There are a few different power options, and I ran it on turbo for most of the cleaning cycle because I have two pets. I felt like the suction power delivered, but it did kill the battery relatively quickly.

Mopping is equally as satisfying, and it took roughly half the time to do all my laminate floors. The QV 35A automatically refills and empties its water reservoir, so I don’t really have to do anything besides turn it on and let it do its thing.

The robot vacuum attempted to work its way over the legs of my kitchen island chairs, and after a few tries, it got stuck. Obstacle avoidance was mostly accurate otherwise, but I had to manually add a no-go zone in the app so the vacuum avoids this spot in the future.

Dyson remains a top brand when it comes to cordless stick vacuums, and I’ve personally tested several of its models. The V15 Detect vacuum comes with a laser cleaner to illuminate hidden dirt, dust, and debris on hardwood floors, and this feature has proved to be very useful for me, even in well-lit rooms. The traditional-style cleaner head works well on carpet, and neither head feels lackluster in suction power.

The cordless-to-handheld structure is nice for going from longer cleaning sessions to quick or more detailed cleaning, and I like using the hair screw tool for removing pet fur from couches, cushions, and more. Better yet, there is a built-in dusting and crevice tool that is great for quick cleanups.

An LCD screen on the handheld portion shows what size of particles you’re cleaning up in real time, along with battery levels and overall cleanliness status. The HEPA filtration is added peace of mind that you’re getting a thorough clean.

Full Dyson V15 Detect Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

If a corded stick or upright vacuum isn’t the best choice for your home cleaning needs, then check out the LVAC-300 from Levoit. It’s a cordless stick vacuum that switches between hard floors, rugs, and tiles without skipping a beat or losing suction power. According to our tester, the vacuum uses three different modes to take on an array of cleaning jobs like picking up cat litter or fine dust, without spreading material around your floors.

It only weighs a little over 6 pounds, so it’s easy to lift and maneuver, and the vacuum lays completely flat for cleaning under furniture. The LED headlight on the floor head illuminates any lingering messes in areas with less visibility.

The LVAC-300 is designed with a five-stage HEPA filter with as much efficiency as an air purifier, and it’s also washable and reusable. The dust container releases with the touch of a button, and it empties just as easily.

We’re keen on the LVAC-300’s handheld vacuum capability and the various attachments it comes with, like a mini motorized brush for couch cushions and beds, and a crevice tool that is slender enough for car seats. A minor inconvenience is that there’s nowhere to store these accessories, which might occasionally interrupt your cleaning session if you have to change tools.

Full Levoit LVAC-300 Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

We recently added the Shark PowerDetect Cordless Stick Vacuum to our cleaning tool arsenal. It looks like something from the future, but it actually solves a lot of the problems cordless stick vacuums face in the present, namely when it comes to maneuverability and small-capacity dustbins.

The flexible center pole bends at a joint, which made it much easier for our tester to get under furniture and in tight spaces around his apartment. This vacuum uses detection technology to automatically adjust suction power based on the type of flooring and size of mess, so you don’t have to change manually and potentially miss spills or hidden debris. The floor head light helped illuminate dirt better, too.

Another useful feature is the docking station. Once our tester was finished cleaning, he locked the vacuum back onto the base, and it automatically suctioned collected dirt, hair, and dust out of the main dustbin. This doesn’t entirely offset the small dustbin capacity on the vacuum itself, but it’s nice not having to manually empty the receptacle after every clean.

Full Shark PowerDetect Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

We have several roundups of vacuums, including cordless stick models and robots. This guide is dedicated to the top overall vacuums we’ve tested, but there are still a few other units worth considering depending on your cleaning needs.

Miele Guard L1: This canister vacuum offers convenience and power for cleaning different floor types. The Classic C1 Turbo Team we recommend above comes with a powered carpet brush, while the L1 does not. It does have longer cable reach and an illuminated display, but the C1 is the better, more affordable selection if you have a mix of surface types in your home.

Shark PowerDetect: This is a buy-up version of the Shark PowerDetect Speed we recommend above. It comes with the same flexible hinge for cleaning under furniture and several intuitive features, including automatic suction adjustment and a cleaner head with LED lights for illuminating dirt. With the regular PowerDetect, you get 10 more minutes of run time and one more level of detection (the vacuum can tell when it’s in a corner or up against a wall and ramp up the suction accordingly). But you get more bang for your buck with the Speed.

Many vacuums are available in both corded and cordless models. Corded vacuums offer unlimited run time, but require a nearby outlet. Cordless or battery-powered models are convenient to use, as you can just pick them up and start cleaning, but they have a limited runtime.

The best option for you depends on how you like to clean—do you vacuum your whole house in one go? If so, go for a corded model. Or do you normally clean one room at a time? Then a cordless option might work just fine for your needs.

Different vacuums are better suited for cleaning hard floors or carpeting, and some feature heads that raise or lower to meet the height of the surface you’re vacuuming. If you have a combination of flooring types, you may want to look for a vacuum with multiple heads and attachments, too.

Vacuum brush rolls, or “beater bars,” come in several different styles, and each is made for specific cleaning tasks and flooring. The most common types you’ll see are bristle, soft, and tangle-free. Bristle rolls are designed with stiff, nylon bristles that are ideal for thick carpets because they lift dirt effectively. They are less optimal on delicate surfaces as their harsh structure causes scratches or other damage.

For hardwood floors, or homes with a mix of surfaces, a vacuum with a soft roll brush is what you need. They’re gentle yet efficient, picking up fine particles without scattering. Tangle-free is best for pet owners, since they resist hair wrapping and are easier to maintain.

Some of today’s vacuums feature dual brush rolls, or have detachable vacuum heads for adjusting to different situations.

Capacity refers to how much dust, dirt, and grime the vacuum can hold before the dustbin needs emptying. Bigger capacities are better for larger homes or heavy-duty cleaning, while smaller dustbins are better for compact spaces or low-lift tasks. Upright vacuums typically have a dustbin capacity of 0.75 liters or more, while stick vacs only hold a couple of quarts at a time.

Maneuverability determines how easily the vacuum navigates around furniture, corners, and other obstacles. Features like swivel steering, lightweight builds, and sturdy wheels all contribute to better control. Typically, vacuums with bigger capacity are more difficult to maneuver around, usually due to a combination of size and weight. Striking the right balance between capacity and maneuverability will help you find a vacuum that’s both efficient and easy to handle.

The suction power of vacuums is commonly measured in Pascals (Pa), a unit that gauges pressure, but some brands—including Dyson—list airwatts, or the watts used by the vacuum to move a unit of air through its nozzle, instead. Not all vacuums have their suction power listed, but when comparing different models, keep in mind that high Pa or airwatts equates to more suction power.

Vacuums vary widely in price ranging from as little as $20 to $1,000 or more. Budget-friendly vacuums tend to have less powerful suction and fewer features, and if it’s a cordless model, its battery life will likely be shorter. Premium vacuums, on the other hand, typically have an ergonomic design that’s more comfortable to operate for longer periods, and their suction power is often noticeably better.

While it’s certainly tempting to give up vacuuming all together, a robot vacuum generally isn’t going to be sufficient to keep your home clean. These vacuums are designed for light-duty cleaning, and they simply can’t match the suction power of a full-size vacuum, especially on carpeting. You might be able to get away with using just a robot vacuum if you have a small home, no pets, and solely hard floors, but I think you’d still find yourself needing another vacuum to clean up occasional messes.

If you have pets, you know that pet hair wreaks havoc on a vacuum. A few passes over a dirty rug, and all of a sudden there’s a wad of hair wrapped around the brush roll, forcing you to stop and untangle it. To avoid problems like this, I highly recommend vacuums designed for pet hair. These models often have anti-tangle brush rolls and good filters, ensuring they capture all the dirt and dander that your furry friends bring into your home.

While often neglected, vacuum cleaner maintenance is key to keeping your machine running properly and ensuring it will last for years to come. You’ll want to make sure you’re emptying the bag or dustbin as often as recommended, as well as washing or replacing filters. Periodically cleaning the brush roll improves suction power, too.

Some vacuums are easier to maintain than others, and you’ll want to be honest with yourself about how much maintenance you’re willing to do—otherwise, your expensive tool might break sooner than expected.

Amber is a Reviews Editor with bylines on Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, and Best Products sites. Specializing in kitchen gadgets, small appliances, lifestyle, and consumer tech, she brings hands-on testing and a detail-oriented approach to every review. In her free time you can likely find her trading trinkets at an EDM festival, searching for hidden gems at thrift stores, or cuddling with her two cats.

The brains of people with PTSD bear molecular changes that differ from those in people with other conditions, like depression, a new study finds.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A study of hundreds of brains has revealed molecular differences in people with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) that are not found in individuals without the condition.

These molecular marks also differ from those seen in the brains of people with other conditions, like depression, the research found.

Our environment and experiences influence how our genes work, affecting which genes can be turned on. Rather than changing genes' underlying code, the environment can trigger what are known as epigenetic changes, which include certain chemicals that attach to DNA molecules and change their structure.

One such epigenetic change, called methylation, can work like a "dimmer switch" for genes, or even completely block certain genes from turning on.

"These epigenetic features of the brain are important for shaping the way the brain functions," study co-author Frances Champagne, a psychologist at the University of Texas at Austin, told Live Science. "This can give us some insight into why individuals with PTSD develop PTSD, or how [their brains] are different from a healthy brain."

In the new study, published Friday (Nov. 20) in the journal Cell Reports, scientists took a close look at DNA methylation in 302 brains that had been donated after death. These included 101 brains from individuals diagnosed with PTSD, 101 from people with major depressive disorder and 100 from people without any diagnosed psychiatric disorders. The researchers also had access to these individuals' medical records.

The team zoomed in on three brain regions: the prefrontal cortex, the amygdala and the hippocampus. The prefrontal cortex handles cognitive functions like planning and decision-making, the amygdala is a major hub for emotional processing, and the hippocampus is key for memory and learning.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"The goal of our study was to look at the epigenetics of the PTSD brain and ask how [it] is different from that of an individual who does not have PTSD," Champagne said, "or who comparatively has another diagnosis, like major depressive disorder."

Compared to the brains of people without any disorders, the brains of people with PTSD had different patterns of methylation in the prefrontal cortex, in particular. By contrast, in major depressive disorder, the amygdala stood out as a brain region with distinct methylation.

Additionally, in depression, the observed differences in methylation tended to affect the same set of genes across different regions of the brain. This was not the case in PTSD, which showed more inconsistencies in terms of which specific genes were involved. The methylation patterns in PTSD also appeared to vary depending on other factors, such as patients' sex, ethnicity and age at which they experienced trauma.

The study's results serve as a valuable resource, said Seyma Katrinli, an investigator in the Grady Trauma Project, a large PTSD study, at the Emory University School of Medicine.

Although the findings can't be used to help diagnose PTSD yet, down the line, this area of research could help scientists correlate changes that are measurable in people's blood to changes in the brain, said Katrinli, who was not involved in the new work. Then, blood tests could help guide the diagnosis and treatment of PTSD, she suggested.

That said, the study had limitations. Because the scientists analyzed postmortem brains, they relied on the medical reports rather than assessing the study subjects directly. Additionally, both PTSD and major depressive disorder are associated with substance use, which also causes DNA methylation; this potential confounding factor was not accounted for in the study. .

Finally, at this point, there is no way to tell what triggered the observed differences in DNA methylation. The scientists can't say if the variations are a consequence of PTSD, a risk factor for PTSD, or a downstream effect of other things that co-occur with PTSD.

The research sets the stage to "help us ask better questions," Champagne said. Her team is now looking to investigate factors — such as sex, the timing of traumatic experiences, or history of substance use — that may be driving the variation within PTSD.

"It's a very exciting foray into epigenetic profiling in the brain," she said.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

DNA methylation profiling of human brain in posttraumatic stress and major depressive disorders indicate specific molecular features. Cell Reports, 118270. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.celrep.2026.118270

#6230. This week: Lame duck kicks off with Hegseth impeachment effort

Departing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

The lame-duck session of Congress kicks off this week as the House is expected to consider a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth while the Senate seeks to advance a bipartisan deal on permitting reform.

Last week’s midterm elections saw Democrats claim sizable majorities in both the House and Senate in the new Congress, and among the immediate questions is whether the demoralized GOP will face attendance woes.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the expected next speaker of the House, said Sunday that he would support the Hegseth impeachment.

“I'm a hard 'yes' on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries said on ABC’s “This Week.” “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe. Pete Hegseth has got to go.”

Departing Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session.

It’s also orientation week on Capitol Hill for new members of Congress. House orientation got underway Sunday.

The Senate, meanwhile, looks to take up a bipartisan permitting bill that has the backing of President Donald Trump.

“This Landmark Permitting Reform Legislation will codify our America First Energy Agenda, and ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families, and creating High Paying American Jobs,” Trump posted on Truth Social.

Senate negotiators over the weekend released text of an amendment seeking to address remaining concerns.

“I’m grateful for the input throughout this process from Senate and House colleagues, environmental and labor organizations, and Tribal leaders. Our manager’s amendment improves [the bill] and addresses the thoughtful feedback we have received,” Senate Environment and Public Works ranking Democrat Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island said in a statement. “Now it’s time to pass this bill so we can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build big things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of new well-paying union jobs.”

Beyond the permitting bill, the Senate Republican majority may seek to use its remaining time trying to confirm more of Trump’s nominations before the control of the floor agenda passes to the Democrats.

"We've got the farm bill, the NDAA, and we have that third reconciliation bill that we need to get across the finish line, and there are so many things that we need to get done and buttoned up," including nominations, departing Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., said in a weekend Fox News interview. Blackburn, one of the Republicans who had success at the ballot box, is now governor-elect of Tennessee. But it's an open question how long lawmakers will want to stick around.

There’s also the matter of an imminent fight over funding the government and laying the groundwork for the new Congress. Republican leadership elections are scheduled for Tuesday, while Democratic leadership elections are expected in December. Democratic senators-elect are due on Capitol Hill Monday and Tuesday, according to the office of Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. Schumer is widely expected to be the majority leader in 2027.

There have been some calls for Senate Republicans to delay their elections, though current Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota has been widely expected to remain as the Republican leader.

“One of the things I learned in business and the Army is that after a failure, you have to start with honesty, transparency, and accountability,” Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa., said in a Sunday night statement. “As I’ve shared with Leader Thune, I don’t believe we should move to leadership elections until we have digested and debated the lessons of the midterms and how to move forward.”

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., has also been circulating a letter calling for a delay, and he has argued the election should not be held, in part, because the makeup of the Senate Republican Conference is not yet final. Senate races are still not called in Alaska and Mississippi.

Absent this week will be Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who recently had a stroke.

“The doctors are very encouraged by the progress I’ve made so far. In order to take my recovery seriously and get back to work on the quickest timeline possible, I will be spending several weeks at a rehabilitation center after being discharged from the hospital today,” Murphy said in a Friday statement.
