#6229. 11 Warm-Weather Destinations to Flock to This Winter

Arguably the best way to overcome winter is to pretend like it’s not happening—i.e., jetting off to a warm-weather destination, where seasons are not taken very seriously and an outdoor adventure is always on the table. The best winter vacation destinations offer comfortable temperatures, off-peak advantages, and festive happenings. On this list, you’ll find some of the usual suspects, from Punta Cana to the US Virgin Islands, as well as locales you might not have considered (far too often, travelers forget vibrant Marrakech is a shorter-haul Mediterranean option).

Whether you’re interested in hiking to the wild and wondrous waterfalls of Puerto Rico’s El Yunque National Rainforest, snorkeling through the kaleidoscopic waters of Belize’s barrier reef, or simply want to kick back and relax with a dip in Costa Rica’s hot springs, these sunny locations are bound to cure those cold-weather blues. So, trade your snow boots for flip-flops and get to plotting your next escape.

When to go: JanuaryAverage winter temperature: 80–85 degrees

If you’ve been looking for an excuse to finally book that trip to Hawaii, shoot for after the holiday rush, when flights get significantly cheaper. January might be the start of rainy season in Maui, but the showers are often short and localized; for the most part, you’ll enjoy sunshiny days with temperatures that hover in the low-80s. Humpback whales make their way from Alaska around this time, and you can spot the giant beauties from Papawai Point on Honoapiilani Highway, an overlook facing the ʻAuʻau Channel. If you’re not afraid of big waves, heavy north swells at this time of year make for excellent surfing, especially at Ho‘okipa Beach Park. The Road to Hana, a scenic and beautiful drive at any time of year, becomes especially lush in the winter after the rain has fallen, and you’ll likely avoid the crowds too. Along the way, hit up sites like the Twin Falls or the black sand beach at Waianapanapa State Park.

Where to stay: A Condé Nast Traveler Triple Crown winner, Hāna-Maui Resort, a luxurious off-grid escape, is the pot of gold at the end of the Road to Hana, while Hotel Wailea offers an adults-only vibe on the southwestern coast. Though much humbler, Jimi Hendrix’s former gingerbread-style home, now available for rent on Airbnb, is also a fair contender for your home away from home, surrounded by all kinds of fruit trees and perfectly positioned for daily rainbows.

When to go: December–JanuaryAverage winter temperature: 65 degrees

While you won’t be breaking a sweat in San Diego come December, it’s an excellent place to escape to around the holidays for festive fun in mild, mid-60-degree temperatures. The Parade of Lights is a classic seasonal event, when over 100 private boats get decked out in twinkling lights and sail around San Diego Bay (watch from spots like Shelter Island or Seaport Village on select nights in December). Between November and January, you can also enjoy ice skating without the chill at the Hotel del Coronado, where you’ll glide alongside the Pacific. They say San Diego sunsets are best in the winter, when the sun cuts a path closer to the horizon and there’s not as much coastal marine fog—one of the best places to catch one is Sunset Cliffs Natural Park on the Point Loma peninsula.

Where to stay: La Valencia, otherwise known as the “Pink Lady” of La Jolla, is one of San Diego’s most iconic stays, and you might hear a seal or two barking in the distance. For unparalleled mountain views, consider this glass house overlooking Sweetwater Regional Park.

When to go: December–MarchAverage winter temperature: 70–85 degrees

For a Caribbean escape with outdoor adventure, cultural festivals, and farm-to-table splendor, head to Puerto Rico. From December to March, you can take advantage of the dry season on the island, which means your days won’t be interrupted by sudden showers. Holiday festivities continue well beyond Christmas, from Three Kings Day on January 6—the oldest of these celebrations takes place in Juana Díaz, with a reenactment of the Magi on horseback—to the San Sebastian Street Festival, when the namesake street in Old San Juan is filled with art vendors, live music, and plenty of mofongo (January 21–24 this year). Winter is also a great time to explore El Yunque National Forest when it’s not shrouded in unbearable humidity—hike to La Coca Waterfall, take in the green canopy from Yokahú Tower, and keep an ear out for singing coquí frogs.

Where to stay: For luxe accommodations just a 25-minute drive from El Yunque, look no further than Four Seasons Resort and Residences Puerto Rico, which coordinates guided treks with a strong emphasis on Indigenous history. Condado Ocean Club offers direct access to the beach, while this lakefront retreat near Cueva Ventana and Arecibo Observatory is ideal for couples seeking verdant views.

When to go: December–MarchAverage winter temperature: 85 degrees

Another destination where US travelers can leave their passports at home, the US Virgin Islands are a quintessential Caribbean paradise. December through March is peak season, and there are plenty of reasons why—no rain, calm seas, and temperatures that hover between 77 and 85 degrees, to name a few. St. Croix, the largest of the USVI’s three main islands, is defined by the white sands of Rainbow Beach, as well as its Danish ancestry, which you can explore at colonial-era sites like Fort Frederik and Fort Christiansvaern. St. John is filled with all kinds of natural wonders; take the Underwater Snorkel Trail at Trunk Bay to peer at parrotfish, or set off on the three-mile Reef Bay Trail to hike among pre-Columbian petroglyphs painted by Taíno Indians. St. Thomas is a bustling port with cosmopolitan charm, and you’d be well advised to sample a few conch fritters at Gladys' Café. Whichever island you choose, clear skies and turquoise waters await.

Where to stay: One of Traveler’s favorite private island resorts (and the only one in the US Virgin Islands), Lovango Resort and Beach Club is located across St. John’s Caneel Bay and offers all kinds of eco-chic accommodations, from wooden treehouses to explorer-style tents. The Westin St. Thomas is set right in front of the harbor, with a stellar spa worth traveling for. For something a bit more intimate, this light-filled, two-bedroom cottage is just a five-minute walk away from Cruz Beach.

When to go: December–FebruaryAverage winter temperature: 65 degrees

While temperatures do drop in Marrakech during the winter—the peaks of the Atlas Mountains will be blanketed in snow—you’ll see far more sun than in certain parts of the US; plus, it’s all the more reason to enjoy a steamy hammam. Winter is a great time to explore the city's popular sites with thinner crowds: comb through the medina’s bustling souks for fragrant spices and a pair of babouche slippers, take in the cobalt blue buildings at the Jardin Majorelle, or learn about one of France’s most legendary fashion designers at the Yves Saint Laurent Museum. Keep an eye out for the dates of the Marrakech International Film Festival, which takes place between the months of November and December—this year it falls from November 20 to 28, and features 76 films from 39 countries.

Where to stay: Traveler contributor Jordan Lippe-McGraw is a big fan of this family-friendly villa, with a heated pool, hammam, and cinema room. A Triple Crown winner, La Mamounia is the city’s grand dame. As global features director Erin Florio puts it, “Every inch of this palatial property has been hyper-considered to make the guest feel as though they have arrived in some regal estate of an Arabian kingdom.” At the Royal Mansour, all riads come with 24/7 access to a private butler.

When to go: December–AprilAverage winter temperature: 80–90 degrees

The Arenal Volcano looms over Costa Rica’s La Fortuna region, heating its natural springs, and there’s a greater chance you’ll see it without cloud cover in the winter. For travelers seeking a combo of adventure and relaxation, La Fortuna (about a three-hour drive from San José) is well-suited for both. Hike through cooled lava fields at Arenal Volcano National Park or swim around La Fortuna Waterfall, then take advantage of nature’s healing powers at Tabacón Thermal Resort and Spa. For a truly memorable experience, book a tour with Arenal Horse Tours and ride your steed straight into the Arenal River for a refreshing dip.

Where to stay: While Tabacón is perhaps the most iconic resort in the area, The Springs Resort & Spa is another great option, boasting two dozen hot springs, pools, and waterfalls spread across the 65-acre property. If you’re looking for something more intimate, this forest cabin features a private spring-fed pool, rain shower, and marked hiking trails—a one-of-a-kind off-grid retreat.

When to go: December–AprilAverage winter temperature: 80–85 degrees

Though small, this Central American country offers a diversity of experiences, whether you want to take it slow in a charming fishing village or ascend new heights in the jungle. Perhaps the most popular destination on Belize’s tourism map, Ambergris Caye is a departure point for the country’s barrier reef—though just south of Ambergris Caye, Caye Caulker provides a nice alternative. While on the car-free island, book a tour with Ragga Sail Adventures for a half-day snorkel through Hol Chan Marine Reserve, the oldest marine reserve in the country. Further south in Punta Gorda, you’ll find rugged adventures and a strong sense of Mayan culture. Here, you’ll have access to several offshore cayes (Belize has hundreds of these small islands, brimming with marine life), from Snake Cayes to Sapodilla Cayes Marine Reserve; if you prefer jungle, take a boat tour through the Monkey River, or hike to the waterfall at Rio Blanco National Park. And be sure to explore the surrounding Toledo District for Mayan ruins, like the Lubaantun, which dates back to 700–900 AD and is also an excellent site for birdwatching.

Where to stay: Nestled within the Belizean rainforest, Copal Tree Lodge’s jungle suites will make you feel as though you’re suspended among the trees. Wake up to the sounds of monkeys every morning, then take a farm tour around the surrounding property, where you’ll discover how cacao, vanilla, and sugar cane grow. Over in San Pedro, Alaia Belize is your luxury option, just 600 yards away from the barrier reef, while this tiny home will make you feel as though you’re vacationing in a fairy tale.

When to go: December–AprilAverage winter temperature: 80 degrees

December through April is peak vacation time in Punta Cana, when the rainy season has subsided and there’s not a cloud in the sky. With average highs in the 80s and average lows in the 70s, you’re likely to experience perfect weather during your stay. Come February, you’ve got a good chance of spotting some humpback whales if you cast your eyes off the coast of the Península de Samaná, where they typically pass through until April. The country also celebrates Independence Day in February—on the 27th, to be exact. Visit around that time, and you’re bound to run into a Carnaval parade or bachata dance circle. With the Cordillera Oriental mountain range looming in the background and a selection of cenotes around town—from Hoyo Azul to Hoyo Claro—mountain buggy excursions and diving adventures await even in the winter.

Where to stay: The W Punta Cana redefines the all-inclusive resort as we know it with top-tier dining and some of the largest rooms in the country. Hyatt Vivid Punta Cana, which just opened its doors in August 2026, is another upscale all-inclusive in the area, boasting swim-out suites and a chic speakeasy. If you’ve got kids in tow but still want to experience the height of luxury, Eden Roc Cap Cana is a consistent Readers' Choice Awards winner. For a villa the whole family will enjoy, this eight-bedroom Airbnb in Tortuga Bay comes with a private pool.

When to go: December–AprilAverage winter temperature: 70 degrees

Another prime location for whale watching, Baja California’s southern tip sees the migration of humpback and gray whales between the months of December and April (you might even elect to swim with whale sharks, too, which roam around the nearby Bay of La Paz around this time). You’ll have just missed the rainy season in November, making way for sunny, 70-degree beach days and not-too-chilly evenings. The creative town of Todos Santos boasts a number of art galleries to pop into, like Galeria de Todos Santos and La Sonrisa de la Muerte, while the Sierra de la Laguna mountains are home to stunning trails and swimming holes. If you’re a surfer, Playa Los Cerritos and Playa San Pedro offer some of Mexico’s best waves.

Where to stay: Todos Santos is home to a number of cutting-edge boutique hotels. Hotel San Cristobal, with its vibrant interiors and delectably fresh seafood, perfectly embodies the bohemian vibes of this tiny surf town. Paradero Todos Santos, located on a five-and-a-half-acre farm, is designed around outdoor adventure: Pick the “Unbound” option, and surfing, hiking, and biking experiences will all be included in the nightly fare. If you prefer to go the rental route, this little bungalow is set among farmland in Pescadero, with its own private rooftop.

When to go: December–FebruaryAverage winter temperature: 75 degrees

Miami is a good idea any time of year, but December through February is considered the dry season, promising temperatures in the mid-70s. Two important events pop up this time of year: Art Basel Miami, in December (4–6, this year), and the South Beach Wine & Food Festival, in February (running the 25–28 in 2027). But there’s always something to do in the Magic City, whether that’s taking a peek into the Pérez Art Museum, spending money in the Design District, or having a stroll through the Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden.

Where to stay: To embrace the happy-go-lucky spirit of the locals, check in to the Goodtime Hotel and sip on a Purple Reign cocktail (co-owner Pharrell’s favorite drink) at the rooftop pool club. If you’d like to tap into the city’s Art Deco architectural history, stay at The Moore, where you’ll be close to Wynwood and Downtown Miami. This dreamy loft in Collins Park, just a short walk to the beach, is a good bet too.

When to go: December–FebruaryAverage winter temperature: 85 degrees

Depending on where you’re coming from, Cape Town might be a little out of the way. But the US's winter is their summer, and with that comes sunny days and a dry, Mediterranean-like climate. Around mid-January, tourists start to flee and kids return to school, making popular attractions more accessible. Take a cable car (or hike, if you’re feeling bold) up to the famous Table Mountain, or drive to Boulders Beach, which boasts one of the last colonies of African penguins in the world. There are plenty of opportunities to engage with some art, as well, from the contemporary galleries at Zeitz MOCAA to the rainbow houses of the Bo-Kaap Museum. And if you’re feeling especially adventurous, you can treat Cape Town as a jumping-off point for the famed Garden Route road trip.

#6228. A fast-growing heart is good for the Grinch. People are another story

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Unlike in the Dr. Seuss tale, a swollen heart can be an alarming sign of stress or disease

The Grinch’s change of heart turned him from grumpy to radiating joy. Is such a transformation possible in real life?

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In the classic Dr. Seuss tale, How the Grinch Stole Christmas, the Grinch starts out with a heart “two sizes too small.” He’s a mean one, disguising himself as Santa Claus and stealing all the Whos’ toys, food and decorations. Poised to throw it all off a mountain, the grumpy loner has a change of heart as joyous song rises from Whoville.

“They say that the Grinch’s small heart grew three sizes that day,” giving him “the strength of 10 Grinches plus two,” says the narrator of the 1966 movie version. With a beatific smile, he pulls the stolen goods back from the brink and returns everything.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Would a too-small heart make you grumpy like the Grinch? And what would happen if your heart went from too small to really big in an instant? The answer depends on what causes the heart to shrink or swell, experts say. And whether or not you are a snake.

Heart size is generally pegged to body size, says Michelle Kittleson, a cardiologist at Cedars Sinai Smidt Heart Institute in Los Angeles. Bigger people tend to have bigger hearts. But some people, she says, have hearts that are naturally bigger or smaller than average for their bodies. It’s not clear why. However, she says, “there are negative consequences of having a too-small heart.”

In one 2025 study, researchers looked at medical records from more than 360,000 people in Australia. Those with smaller-than-average hearts had a higher risk of dying within five years than people with average or larger hearts, the team reported in JACC: Advances.

Smaller hearts may not pump blood as well as larger ones, making it harder for people to exercise. And if the Grinch didn’t exercise enough, maybe “then that made him really tired, and that made him grumpy,” Kittleson says. “Or maybe he did the research, and he found out that his life expectancy was shortened because of it, and that made him even grumpier.”

But would rapidly increasing his heart’s size be good for the Grinch?

As the Grinch slides downhill toward Whoville, pulled by a sled piled high with presents he’d stolen and now was returning, he physically undergoes a change. What started as a heart two sizes too small swelled three sizes, both curing his grumpiness and giving him super strength. Or so the classic tale goes. A person going through such a dramatic change may not fare as well.

There are many ways a heart can grow, says Leslie Leinwand, a molecular biologist and geneticist at the University of Colorado Boulder. With vigorous exercise, “your heart gets bigger in good ways,” Leinwand says. That can be true for athletes who do lots of cardio, such as swimmers and marathon runners.

“Their heart gets bigger and thicker,” Kittleson says. “But it’s a good thing in them because it helps them pump more blood per minute than someone with a normal-size heart.” Pregnancy also makes the whole organ expand to boost blood to the developing fetus. If people stop exercising, or give birth, their hearts will shrink back to normal size within months.

Some diseases, though, can enlarge hearts in deadly ways. “If you’ve got untreated high blood pressure,” Leinwand says, “you can get a huge heart, and it’s not good for you.”

Stress, bad heart valves and some genetic diseases can also result in bigger, but weaker, hearts. In those cases, the heart muscle grows in order to pump more blood. At the same time, the inside of the left ventricle — the heart chamber that pumps oxygenated blood to the body — can shrink. That makes it harder for the heart to push blood out. This kind of growth takes time, Kittleson says.

There is one rare condition in which the heart can inflate suddenly. Called takotsubo or stress cardiomyopathy — or in some cases, broken-heart syndrome — it is brought on by extreme stress. That can include positive things like winning the lottery or entering a surprise party or negative stress such as break-up or losing a job.

A surge of epinephrine, or adrenaline, from stress can make the left ventricle bulge into the shape of a pot used to catch octopuses. (Takotsubo is Japanese for “octopus pot.”) That causes immediate heart failure as the heart chamber gets too big to pump blood.

So instead of becoming super strong, the Grinch “would have keeled over and collapsed,” Kittleson says. (People can survive with prompt medical care and their hearts can return to normal size in a few months.)

Given the Grinch survived his rapid growth, there’s another possible scenario: Maybe his heart is more like a snake’s.

Pythons’ hearts can balloon by up to 25 percent in a day after the snakes eat a large meal — sometimes as big as an adult deer. And the bigger a python’s meal, the more its heart grows. Larger hearts pump blood with more force, Leinwand and her colleagues reported in 2024 in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The researchers don’t know if this makes the snakes stronger overall.

Once a meal is digested, the heart shrinks again. Snakes can go through many shrink-and-grow cycles with no ill effect. Leinwand hopes that studying these snakes will lead to treatments that make human hearts healthier.

But becoming kinder, like the Grinch? Maybe not.

Notes Leinwand, “our snakes, when they eat a lot, they get rather aggressive.”

#6227. Scientists Studied Thousands of Ancient Skeletons and Found a Strange Truth About Human Progress

Over 7,000 years, height rose and fell across Europe and Asia. Food quality, not tech, made the difference.

The dairy industry’s “Milk. It does a body good” slogan has some historical backing, at least in Europe. That’s one of the more surprising takeaways from a large study that used ancient skeletons to track how well people lived across Europe and Asia over the past 7,000 years. The researchers based their analysis on one telling measurement: human height.

“When children and adolescents have access to sufficient, high-quality food, they grow taller, within the constraints of genetic factors,” Manon Stephan, an economic historian at Germany’s University of Tübingen, said in a statement. “Therefore, height enables us to draw conclusions about living standards.”

To test that idea, Stephan and colleagues at Tübingen and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology examined 18,457 bones from 783 sites in 45 countries. In the study, published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the team estimated people’s heights from their long bones. They then tracked how average height changed in each region and compared those changes with shifts in population density and technology.

In China, men were taller 7,000 years ago, averaging 5 feet 10 inches. Over time, however, their height steadily declined, reaching a low of just 5 feet 3 inches on average in the 19th century. Chinese women’s height also declined, though less drastically, falling from an average of 5 feet 2 inches 7,000 years ago to 4 feet 10 inches in more recent times.

Trends like these would be nearly impossible to trace through written records alone. “In many parts of the world, any written sources that would allow us to draw conclusions about economic development appear quite late on our timeline and are patchy in their distribution,” Stephan said. “That’s why we rely on bones.” The bones in question came from 22 Asian and 23 European countries and were taken from the graves of commoners in both densely populated and rural regions.

In Europe, by contrast, the trends went in a different direction. Around 5,000 years ago, men in northern Europe averaged just 5 feet 4 inches. However, the study authors wrote, as pastoralist peoples migrated from the steppes of Eastern Europe and western Siberia, they brought with them more advanced dairy farming and the genetic trait of lactose tolerance. This led to greater consumption of dairy products, which the study identifies as a leading factor in increased height. Average heights in northern Europe continued to climb into the early Middle Ages, but sometime between 500 and 1000 C.E., they began to decline, a trend that lasted until the end of the 19th century.

Women’s heights followed a similar pattern. China and Japan experienced the steepest declines, while Europe saw a rise, though a less steep one than among men.

The authors wrote that “human stature is a valuable indicator of nutritional status and health.” Reconstructing this indicator offers insight into which societies provided better health and nutrition to their people. Surprisingly, technological progress did not prove to be a major factor in improving either.

“Our study also confirmed that technological progress does not automatically lead to greater height,” said Jörg Baten, a professor of economic history at the University of Tübingen. “In China, for example, new, higher-yielding rice varieties and other innovations were introduced in the 11th century [C.E.]. While the higher yields enabled the empire to remain the dominant power, they did not subsequently lead to a better standard of living for the general population. Instead, population density increased: People had more children because this was seen as a form of security in old age. This meant, however, that each individual had not more to eat, but less. And importantly the quality declined, for example, in terms of high-quality protein.”

Europe’s findings on technology mirrored Asia’s. Improved technology helped support denser populations, but it didn’t increase average height or necessarily improve the nutritional value of food.

Going forward, the authors hope to link more of these changes in height to shifts in social conditions or developments in agriculture. “This requires further research,” said Mark Hudson, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology. “However, the statistical data reveal trends and provide clues as to when these changes occurred.”

Wolves howl for a variety of reasons. But none of them are triggered by the sight of the moon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Wolves can bark, whimper, yip, squeak and growl, but they are most known for their iconic howl.

The eerie sound can travel vast distances and, if heard by other wolves, get them to join in with the chorus. But why do wolves howl in the first place?

Experts told Live Science that the behavior is triggered not by the sight of the moon, as is commonly believed, but by the need to maintain a complex social network.

Wolves can howl by themselves and in groups. "If a lone wolf howls, it's probably because they're separated from their pack and want to regain contact," Arik Kershenbaum, a zoologist at the University of Cambridge, told Live Science. "Members of a pack can become quite dispersed, and when they need to hunt together, or to care for pups, or when their territory is being threatened by other wolves, they need a way of returning to each other."

However, lone wolves that leave their packs may howl as well. This could be "a way of finding a new pack or mate to join," Kershenbaum said.

When a wolf pack howls together, they are sometimes advertising their territory to deter other packs. "Data shows that packs howl more in the center of their territory; they howl more when there are pups around and also when they have a carcass from a hunt," Tamás Faragó, an ethologist and bioacoustician at Eötvös Loránd University in Budapest, Hungary, told Live Science. "So group howling can have a repellent effect on neighboring packs."

However, "most chorus howling is social — that is, they howl together to build what is technically called social cohesion," Kershenbaum said, "because it makes them feel good to be safe and surrounded by their pack mates. Faragó noted that this kind of group howling gets a pack in the same mood, "and is quite common before going out on a hunt."

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

Howling can trigger more howling. "When an individual wolf hears a howl, it has a very strong tendency to reply back," Faragó said. However, "if a lone wolf is accidentally wandering into the territory of its neighbors, and they hear the pack there howling, they won't respond. That would make it obvious that it's an intruder there."

A wolf's howl can be heard up to 10 miles (16 kilometers) away in open terrain, according to the Wolf Conservation Center in South Salem, New York. The combination of low- and high-frequency sounds that make up howls ensures that "even if some of the lower-frequency sounds are attenuated by vegetation, the higher-frequency components can remain intact and carry a lot of information about the individuals that made the howls," Faragó said.

Wolf pups make their first high-pitched attempts at howling between 2 to 4 weeks old.

Wolf howls differ among species and subspecies. A 2016 study of 13 species and subspecies of wolves, jackals, coyotes and dogs by Kershenbaum and his colleagues found that each has a kind of howling dialect that features different types of howls with varying regularity depending on the species or subspecies. For example, the howling repertoire of the timber wolf (Canis lycaon) is dominated by low, flat howls, while red wolves (Canis rufus) most frequently use high, looping howls.

The howling of dogs, which are descended from gray wolves (Canis lupus), can differ from wolf howling, but this depends very much on the breed. A 2023 study from Kershenbaum, Faragó and their colleagues found that more ancient dog breeds that are more closely related to wolves howl more often. In contrast, more modern dog breeds bark more often.

A question "that we all want to answer" is whether howling sounds might differ depending on their purpose, Kershenbaum said. "The problem is that most of the time when wolves howl, we don't know what they're doing at that time — they're either too far away, or it's nighttime."

Generally, "we believe that howls made in different emotional states probably sound different," Kershenbaum said. "For example, perhaps when a wolf is feeling threatened in a territorial conflict, the howl goes up and down in pitch in a different way than when the wolf is relaxed. But this is a field of active research."

A common belief is that wolves howl at the moon. "A myth, I'm afraid," Kershenbaum said. "There doesn't seem to be any correlation at all between them." He suggested that perhaps before electric lights, people were outdoors more often when there was a bright moon, "and that's when they heard the wolves."

#6225. ‘Political malpractice’: Calls grow to delay Senate GOP leadership elections

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., walks through the Ohio Clock Corridor this summer. Now he’s pushing to delay leadership elections for his conference, urging a discussion of last week’s larger than expected losses. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

After last week’s midterm elections saw them lose at least seven Senate seats and the majority, some Republicans are pushing for a reckoning, saying the conference should stop and think about its future.

“After the stunning defeat [we] just can’t continue on business as usual. That kind of defeat demands change,” Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said on Monday evening.

Asked if he himself would want to run for Senate minority leader, the Wisconsin Republican responded with a question of his own: “That’s part of our problem. Who’d want the job? Would you want it?”

Though no hopeful had emerged as of Monday afternoon — at least publicly — to challenge current Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., for the top GOP post, the frustration was palpable as Republican senators returned to D.C. and grappled with the election results. Calls grew throughout the day to delay the conference’s leadership elections planned for Tuesday morning.

“Well, I mean, I’m open to hearing what the arguments are for that,” Thune told reporters Monday when asked about the possibility of postponing the leadership votes. “I don’t know if that solves anything, but like I said, it’s going to be a decision that’s ultimately made by Republican senators. We’ll hear them out.”

Johnson told reporters on Monday that if the election is held, he would “leave the room” and walk out. Either way, he seemed certain to at least get a “fulsome” discussion of the topic, as he requested in a letter he sent to Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark. Four other Republican senators signed on to the letter, hitting the threshold to call a conference meeting under internal GOP rules.

Also signed by Sens. Mike Lee of Utah, Ted Budd of North Carolina, Rick Scott of Florida, and John Kennedy of Louisiana, the letter obtained by CQ Roll Call cites last week’s “stunning defeat” and reads in part: “Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice.”

Kennedy said Monday evening that he was asking to postpone the leadership elections because “we need time to talk to each other.”

“We’re like a shop owner who’s losing his customers. It’s not the customer’s job to fix that. It’s the shop owner’s job, and I’m not looking for blame-shifting. I’m looking for self-examination,” he said, adding that he wouldn’t consider running for minority leader himself.

In the letter, the group asked that at the time the leadership elections were set to begin, 9 a.m. on Tuesday, they instead “have a fulsome conference discussion and delay holding leadership elections until we all have a chance to hear from leadership candidates as to what type of collaborative conference governing model we should adopt and what our strategy will be to counter the emboldened Democrats.”

Thune echoed that wording Monday as he spoke to reporters, saying, “I do think that we need to have a very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here, and then we’ll see what the consensus of the conference is.”

But Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who serves as chair of the Senate Republican Policy Committee, said she has seen such requests launched in the past and didn’t think it would do much to affect the ultimate outcome. “I think Sen. Thune will be reelected,” she said.

And several Senate GOP aides said that they suspected a “robust” conversation wouldn’t do much to delay the plans and that leadership elections were still expected to take place Tuesday. They noted similar efforts from some of those same senators in previous years to sow discord in the ranks.

That includes Scott, who unsuccessfully challenged Thune in 2024 and then-GOP leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., in 2022. But Scott told Fox News over the weekend, “I don’t want to run again. I’ve run twice.”

Republicans “failed. We had a horrible night,” Scott said. “Instead of having an [leadership] election, the first thing you do is you say, ‘OK, what are we going to change? We have to change something.’”

Lee floated the idea of waiting until after the uncalled Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska are officially resolved.

An online pressure campaign was building in some of the same MAGA corners of the internet that have pushed to pass a sweeping voter ID bill, known as the SAVE America Act, that has stalled in the Senate. On Monday morning, influencer Scott Presler in an X post urged constituents to call their senators while praising the lawmakers who have already pushed for the leadership elections to be postponed. “Where is everyone else?” he wrote.

Sens. Jim Banks of Indiana and Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania also called for a delay, though they did not appear on Johnson’s letter.

“A week ago, we had the worst election results in decades,” McCormick said in a post on X, calling Tuesday “too soon” to vote for leaders. “I know it’s been practice to go straight to leadership elections in recent years, but we should not rush it.”

Banks similarly said Tuesday was “too soon,” posting on social media, “Our conference needs to sit down and have a frank conversation about where we fell short, what we stand for, and what we’re going to do for the working families who sent us here.”

One senator speaking out in Thune’s defense was Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who competed with Thune for the top spot in 2024 but on Monday said the leader isn’t to blame for the midterm results.

“I think the president needs to look in the mirror and look at the flawed candidates that he endorsed, and the kind of environment that we’re in,” said Cornyn, who is still smarting from losing his primary to a challenger backed by President Donald Trump.

Cornyn’s loss means he has no say in the coming conference leadership elections. But he said, “I think Thune’s a good man, and did as well as he could against a president and an environment that was pretty hostile.”

#6224. The 6 Best Smart Thermostats to Keep Your House Comfortable and Save You Money

Get more efficient heating and cooling with these set-it-and-forget-it models.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Just like Wi-Fi-enabled lights and plugs and locks, smart thermostats give you the ability to automate an element of your home for increased convenience. In this case, it’s your temperature controls. These devices tend to be a bit pricier than conventional thermostats, but it’s an upgrade that can pay for itself over time thanks to increased energy efficiency.

Using a companion app on your phone, you get intuitive and nuanced controls, including the ability to customize temperature schedules remotely. That comes in handy when, let’s say, you want to warm up the house earlier than usual if you head home from work early. You’re also able to track your usage with monthly energy reports, which can help you bring down your bills.

For the past few months, my colleagues and I have been steadily testing smart thermostats throughout in our homes, including models from Google Nest, ecobee, and Honeywell Home. These are the models we tried, plus a few more we recommend based on our research and reviews. We’ve also included some expert advice on what to consider before you buy.

The ecobee covers the standard lineup of smart thermostat features, with climate control and money-saving that are commonplace among any of the top options, but sets itself apart with a wider range of smart features.

It doubles as a security base for your home security, serving as the arming and disarming mechanism. It also features a built-in air quality monitor that alerts you to poor air quality and sends reminders when you need to replace air filters in your furnace.

The ecobee comes with a separate smart sensor for precision control, allowing it to fine-tune the temperature in the rooms where you spend the most time. Though it comes with a single sensor, you can purchase more to add that precision throughout the house.

It also provides free Eco+ Software which works on your smartphone and generates energy reports that further maximize your energy savings.

The smart thermostat also comes with a host of standard smart features. After connecting to a Google assistant or Alexa, the smart speaker built directly on the thermostat itself can take voice commands and even play music. It also comes with a three-year warranty from date of purchase.

Each purchase comes with a full converter kit as well, so if you aren’t currently in a home with a C-Wire, you can add one by following the kit instructions.

For a smart thermostat that better fits a tight budget, Amazon has its own option that comes with many of the same energy-saving features at a lower overall price tag. Through the connected app, the thermostat tracks and reports your energy usage and peak time periods throughout the week and month.

Through Alexa, you can also set home, away, and sleep temperatures that you can schedule throughout the day and week in order to further maximize savings on your energy bill and optimize your air conditioning to your exact schedule. You can also set the temperature remotely from your phone through the Alexa app.

Beyond the controls, by using an Amazon product, the company will pass along potential rebate and saving opportunities that you could take advantage of by owning a smart thermostat.

As for upfront costs, the device is designed specifically for easy DIY installation so there is no need to hire an HVAC technician unless you want one.

The Honeywell T9 is a great choice if your primary concern is reducing energy use and lowering your bills. You need to pair it with one of Honeywell’s smart room sensors to take advantage of the thermostat’s full functionality, which is an extra hurdle, but the sensor only costs about $30, so it’s a short one.

One of the key ways the T9 saves money is through virtual fencing. Using your phone’s GPS, the thermostat automatically switches between home and away mode as you come and go. So, when you leave your house, energy usage is reduced across the board.

Honeywell also provides monthly usage reports that point out areas where energy can be reduced for a lower upfront cost. Adding more room sensors can increase the accuracy of those reports, giving you more chances to optimize your heating and cooling system.

The Honeywell T9 doesn’t have the same wide spectrum of features as our other recommendations, but it’s core functionality is very solid.

The newest generation of the Google Nest Thermostat has impressed our team as an easy-to-install, easy-to-use option that reduces energy use and is compatible with most HVAC systems. Like previous models, the smart thermostat builds a schedule, learns your temperature preferences, and reduces energy when it isn’t needed.

Reviews Editor Danny Perez installed the Nest in his own home and absolutely fell in the love with nearly every aspect of it. “To say I like this thermostat is an understatement: It lights up when I pass by to show me the interior temps, as well as local weather and humidity (it’s nice to know my presence is acknowledged, not gonna lie),” writes Perez.

Beyond the basic features, Perez also pointed out how much he likes the actual display and design of the thermostat. “Sure, other thermostats and window a/c units have similar smart features, but they don’t blend into my home the way the Google Nest thermostat does. I genuinely enjoy looking at it. I light up when I pass by it.”

With a large, responsive touch screen, this basic Honeywell thermostat is easy to see from across the room, thanks to a large, custom-color display. It’s a versatile option, compatible with multiple smart home assistants. Like other models, it’s Energy Star-certified, which means that using one can help you save even more money through local rebates.

While the smart thermostat is great for easy scheduling and reading, it lacks the learning software of the Google Nest or the virtual fencing adjustments that many other smart thermostats have. That said, it’s also considerably cheaper.

Most smart thermostats aren’t compatible with baseboard heating and cooling systems. This Mysa unit is the rare exception, and designed specifically to work with electric baseboards. Combine that with compatibility across every major smart home system, and the Mysa becomes one of very few thermostats with such capabilities.

While the compatibility alone makes this a tempting choice, it also has many of the same high-end smart features as the competition. This includes virtual fencing, so when you head out for the day, the thermostat automatically reduces energy use.

Another key feature is its temperature monitor. Unlike many other devices, which only provide you with degrees, the Mysa smart thermostat also measures and reports humidity levels.

Traditional thermostats only require power through the four classic wires while smart thermostats typically require low- voltage power all day in order to run the display screen and some basic functions. This low-voltage power comes from an additional fifth wire called the “common” wire or C-Wire. The biggest potential issue you may have with installation is if your home lacks this wire.

If this is the case, it’s probably time to step away from your weekend home project and call an HVAC technician. While installing a common wire isn’t an incredibly difficult undertaking if you’re somewhat handy, it’s one that likely requires the expertise of a trained professional.

Some smart thermostats include installation kits that provide equipment and step-by-step instructions for adding a C-Wire to your current wiring. This can be a helpful addition to the handier among us, and may circumvent the need for an HVAC technician entirely, though you may want to keep one waiting in the wings if anything goes wrong.

Once you've wired and installed your smart thermostat, you can connect it to other devices in your home via Wi-Fi or occasionally Z-Wave. Most units are compatible with many major smart home ecosystems. While they’re compatible with many systems, I would still take a moment to check and make sure that a thermostat works specifically with the smart home setup you use at home.

Along with scheduling heating or cooling programs from the convenience of your phone, there are a handful of features that set smart thermostats apart from their traditional counterparts. Most smart models automatically adjust the temperature based on peak usage and some automatically respond to outdoor temperatures and set ideal temperatures indoors.

Other models use geofencing, or virtual fencing technology. This creates a radius around your home and detects how close or far away your smartphone is from it. With this, the smart thermostat eases energy use when you aren’t home, and ramps back up as you reenter the virtual boundary.

Several smart thermostats we cover use external sensors to expand the reach of temperature readings. Setup is typically no more complicated than placing the sensors around the house and syncing them up with the rest of the system.

They’re great for maintaining different temperatures in rooms, like keeping bedrooms and bathrooms warm and offices and laundry rooms cool. More precise temperature control also increases the potential for saving energy. Smart thermostats that include sensors as part of their systems often come with one, though some models require purchasing sensors separately.

The Popular Mechanics Gear Team has tested several of these recommendations over the course of several months, including the ecobee Smart Thermostat Premium and the Google Nest Learning Thermostat. We installed these smart thermostats in our homes, set them up, and used them to keep ourselves warm and cool, as the seasons demanded. We gave them our seal of approval based on ease-of-use, installation process, programmable features, and how well the devices integrated with our smart home assistants, mobile devices, and tablets.

A few thermostats, such as the Honeywell Home Smart Color Thermostat, made the list despite the fact that we haven’t tested them yet. In those cases, we picked options from established brands with the specs and features that are comparable to our tested recommendations, and have received strong reviews from customers at online retailers.

We also prioritized options that were highly compatible with other smart devices and offered convenient features for everyday use. Price rice was a major consideration, as well: We chose models ranging from roughly $160 to $250, ensuring that we recommend a range of options that fit every need and budget.

#6223. How to Spend 3 Perfect Days in Naples

A fascinating, complex, and multi-layered city, Naples is brimming with contradictions. Dilapidated, neglected neighborhoods share city space with splendid palaces and world-beating museums. The city’s origins go back to the ancient Greeks, yet the contemporary art scene here is buzzing. There is a state-of-the-art metro system designed by renowned artists and architects (no wonder, since the traffic is infamously heavy).

I’ve been visiting for over 30 years and have seen huge changes, most of them positive. Naples today is safer, more tourist-friendly, and cleaner than ever before, yet it remains Italy’s most beguiling city. The eating and drinking scene has evolved, there is a much wider choice of places to stay (with Rocco Forte due to open a hotel here in 2027), and museums and monuments have been spruced up and reorganized. In 2027, the America’s Cup will arrive as well.

You could easily spend two weeks in Naples and not see everything. But if you only have three days, start early and be prepared to pack in as much as possible; you can rest once you get home. Here is my advice for how to make the most of it.

You coudl easily spend two weeks in Naples and not see everything—but three days are a delicious taste, too.

Historic Gran Caffè Gambrinus is a perfect place to start your first day, shoulder to shoulder with the locals at the bar for a shot of espresso and a warm cornetto (only tourists sit on the terrace). Just across Piazza Trieste e Trento lies the imposing dark grey and red Palazzo Reale where you can visit the sumptuous Royal Apartments and ornate Teatrino, and on the other side is the Teatro San Carlo, one of Italy’s most prestigious opera houses; opera buffs can book a behind-the-scenes tour, or even better, tickets for a performance.

From the Toledo metro station, you get full immersion in the Stazione d’Arte, a public art project involving some of the greatest contemporary artists and architects who have transformed Naples’ main underground stations into public galleries. Dominated by Oscar Tusquets Blanca’s jaw-dropping mosaic, Toledo is one of the most impressive—but for just the price of a metro ticket (just over $2), you can tour them all.

A quick walk north on Via Toledo leads to Via della Pignasecca, where you can catch the end of the lively morning market with its troughs of slithering, glistening fish and seafood, piles of seasonal fruit and vegetables, and stalls selling everything from tripe to knock-off designer handbags.

Lunch at no-nonsense Trattoria da Nenella near Piazza Carità is a noisy, fun experience; you’ll probably have to queue, but the deep-fried anchovies and meatballs in tomato sauce are worth it, and prices are rock-bottom.

The Cappella Sansevero is home to Giuseppe Sammartino’s sublime 1753 marble Cristo Velato.

After a shot of the best coffee in the city at Café Mexico in Piazza Dante, you can spend the afternoon exploring the grid of streets around the so-called Spaccanapoli, the heart of Roman Neapolis where ancient monuments rub shoulders with street food stalls, tiny grocers, once-grand palazzi, and shops selling tourist trinkets and religious memorabilia. Piazza del Gesù, at the western end, is dominated by the eponymous church and an ornate roccoco ‘guglia’. Just to the east is the Church and Convent of Santa Chiara with a beautiful Gothic interior and a cloister famous for its bright, 18th-century majolica tiles. Close by is Naples’ most celebrated (and most crowded) sight, the Cappella Sansevero, home to Giuseppe Sammartino’s sublime 1753 marble Cristo Velato.

Back on the Spaccanapoli, nip into Gay-Odin (n. 61) for a chocolate gelato and then continue to the vast Duomo where you will be dazzled by the gilt-encrusted Cappella di San Gennaro and the subterranean church of Santa Restituita and its 4th-century baptistery.

Close by are the chapel of Pio Monte della Misericordia with Caravaggio’s seminal Seven Acts of Mercy and crumbling Piazza San Girolamini where Banksy’s Madonna with a Pistol appeared on the back right-hand wall in 2004. San Lorenzo Maggiore is an essential visit if you want to understand multi-layered Naples; under the 13th-century church, ongoing excavations have revealed the astonishing remains of a Greco-Roman city dating back 2,000 years.

A detour down Via San Gregorio Armeno takes you past shops selling pastori or figurines for Christmas cribs. Much of what you see is mass-produced these days, so for the real deal, visit Marco Ferrigno’s workshop at number 10. Continue to leafy Piazza Bellini, a lively evening hub, and bag a terrace table at Café Intramoenia for a Campari spritz—you’ve earned it.

For dinner, Europeo di Mattozzi is a personal favorite for its echoes of elegant old Naples; the classic food is fantastic (try the sublime melanzane alla parmigiana and the pasta with potatoes and provola cheese), the host Alfonso is charming, and your fellow diners are likely to be mostly locals.

Use Castel dell'Ovoa as your launchpad for a classic Neapolitan passeggiata along the wide, traffic-free seafront drag.

Day two starts where it all began. Parthenope—later Neapolis and later still Napoli—was founded more than 2,500 years ago on the tiny island of Megaris, now occupied by the Castel dell’Ovo and the picturesque fishing hamlet of Borgo Marinari. There’s nothing much to see in the castle, but it’s a good launch pad for the classic Neapolitan passeggiata along the wide, traffic-free seafront drag. It’s lined with restaurants and cafés offering tables in the sun for a cappuccino and magnificent views.

The delightful neighbourhood of Chiaia is a criss-cross of pretty cobbled lanes peppered with independent boutiques, cool bars, and tiny restaurants; Via dei Mille and Via dei Filangeri are known for designer clothes and chic galleries. The handmade silk ties at tiny, old-fashioned Marinella make wonderful gifts, and a counter perch at tiny Pescheria Mattiucci is a good choice for a quick seafood lunch with a glass of something chilled and white.

Depending on the weather (and energy levels), one option from here is to head west beyond Mergellina to the upmarket seaside suburb of Posillipo for an afternoon on the beach; sunbeds and umbrellas can be rented at Bagno Sirena.

Or you can hop on the Funicolare di Chiaia and trundle up to leafy Vomero and the panoramic Certosa di San Martino, a Carthusian monastery complex with an ornate church, several museums, two cloisters, and the famous Monk’s Cemetery decorated with marble skulls. It also has knock-out views over the whole waterfront and the Bay of Naples to the Sorrentine Peninsula. The Friggitoria Vomero—one of the city’s few remaining authentic ‘frying shops’—doles out sizzling snacks from 6 p.m. and is conveniently close to the funicolare stop as you head back down the hill.

Chiaia’s quiet lanes morph into a nightlife hub from aperitivo hour on, filling up with smartly dressed locals and visitors in search of a good night out. Cocktail spot per eccellenza is retro-glam Antiquario where the jacketed barmen mix a stonking Negroni. From here it’s a short stroll to tiny Ristorante Dora, open since 1973, for textbook versions of fish and seafood classics such as spaghetti alle vongole (with local clams). Head back to Chiaia for a nightcap; follow your nose and the party crowd.

The atmospheric burial site of Cimitero delle Fontanelle is a respite from the buzzing streets above.

A no-go area for tourists until relatively recently, the dilapidated, densely populated but intriguing Rione Sanità is Naples in the raw. Breakfast at Pasticceria Popella in Via Arena alla Sanità is a must for their sfogliatelle and cream-stuffed ‘fiocchi di neve’ before having a rummage among the market stalls and tiny shops on Via dei Vergini; at n. 19 is the grand entrance to the famous pale green and cream Palazzo dello Spagnuolo with its celebrated ‘flying staircase’ by local architect Ferdinando San Felice.

These shambolic streets are filled with tooting cars, buzzing vespas, and bewildered tourists, but there are hidden artistic gems too: the 2,400 year-old recently restored Ipogeo dei Cristallini, the atmospheric burial site of the Cimitero delle Fontanelle with its piles of skulls and bones; and the labyrinthine Catacombs of San Gaudioso under the basilica of Santa Maria della Sanità.

You can’t visit the Sanità without a meal at Ciro Oliva’s crazy-lively temple to pizza Concettina ai Tre Santi (booking is essential), where the tasting menus offer an endless succession of slices topped with whatever the pizzaiolo dreams up at the time.

Naples’ Archaeological Museum (aka Mann) houses one of the world’s great collections of ancient art and artefacts, and if you only visit one museum, make it this. Must-sees include the monumental Roman sculptures on the ground floor, the collection of ancient erotica in the Gabinetto Segreto, and the dazzling mosaics, wall paintings, and bronzes from Pompeii and Herculaneum.

Afterwards, check out the brilliant selection of exquisite handmade gloves at factory prices in the workshops of Omega, a family glove business that first opened in 1923, before winding up the day in the surprisingly peaceful oasis of the exotic Orto Botanico gardens on traffic-clogged Via Foria.

For a last blast, Grand Hotel Parker’s on the way up to Vomero is the smart place to go. Cocktails and light bites are served on the rooftop terrace while on the floor below, chef Domenico Candela whips up a storm with his two-Michelin-star take on local cuisine to a backdrop of unforgettable views.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6222. The Book Lover’s Gift Guide

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Science News staff loved books about dinosaurs, parenting and numbers in 2026

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Science News staff devoured books of all kinds this year, on topics ranging from ecology and evolution to the human brain and mathematics. We covered it all — even a cookbook! These 10 titles rose to the top of our 2026 reading list and could make great gifts for the book lovers in your life. —  Anna Mattson, Assistant Editor

Big thinkers will love Huge Numbers, a fascinating look into the study of large numbers. “When I think of big numbers, I usually think of a 1 with a lot of zeroes tacked on the end. But the reality is much more complex than I ever imagined,” says senior physics writer Emily Conover. The book, among Conover’s favorites of the year, “provided me with a new appreciation of our number system and the creative ways mathematicians have expanded it to express ever-larger numbers,” she says. “Plus, contemplating unfathomably large figures makes my own concerns seem insignificant.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Staff writer Erin Garcia de Jesús’ favorite book of 2026, The Creatures’ Guide to Caring, will strike a chord with new parents. “Between sleepless nights and poopy diapers, there’s not much to laugh about in the early days of parenting. But I found plenty of humor (and plenty to be grossed out about) in The Creatures’ Guide to Caring,” Garcia de Jesús says. “It’s the perfect book to make anyone, parent or otherwise, feel better that we’re not the only animals struggling with our offspring.”

Merritt R. TuretskyW.W. Norton & Company | $29.99

Adventure seekers will lose themselves in the mesmerizing ecosystems at the heart of Bogland, biomedical sciences writer Aimee Cunningham’s favorite book of the year. Ecologist Merritt R. Turetsky immerses readers in these waterlogged landscapes that are often overlooked and underestimated. “I am firmly on team boglands after reading about the beauty and wonder of these ecosystems,” Cunningham says.

Senior writer Meghan Rosen’s favorite book of 2026 is perfect for anyone interested in — or wary of — health and wellness culture. Morbid exposes the lack of science behind a lot of antiaging advice, such as eating like centenarians do and taking “anti­aging” supplements. “Turns out, a lot of it is just plain bunk,” Rosen says. “Skeptical readers will enjoy Newman’s takedowns, which go down smoothly with a healthy dose of humor.”

Senior neuroscience writer Laura Sanders’ pick for 2026 is a must-read for any expecting mother, new mother or person looking to learn about how pregnancy and motherhood impact the body. “A Mother’s Brain reads like a scientific love letter to moms, who all too often get overlooked,” she says. Author and neuroscientist Susana Carmona “covers the nascent field of matrescence in lively, vivid chapters. And along the way, she convincingly argues that the maternal brain is compelling, wondrous and still mysterious,” Sanders says.

Those who listen to true crime podcasts or wish spooky season lasted all year long will enjoy Exhumed, an exploration of the lore and medical practices leading up to the 19th century New England vampire panic. “Thanks to Mahnke’s gripping prose, I felt like I was in the middle of the action. It was hard to lay the book down,” assistant editor Anna Mattson wrote in her online review. Mattson notes that Exhumed, her favorite read of 2026, is littered with bizarre facts that would be perfect for invigorating dull conversations.

For the anthropologist in your life, try The Story of Stories — a deep dive into how technological upheavals have shaped storytelling throughout history. The author provides what Sanders describes as scattershot history lessons in her online review: “Ashton has a knack for pulling out memorable bits from historical records, scientific studies and other sources for readers.”

Alexis Nikole NelsonSimon & Schuster | $35.00

Conover couldn’t pick just one favorite. For people who enjoy getting creative in the kitchen, she recommends Happy Snacking, Don’t Die! “This cookbook provides such a joyful how-to on foraging and eating wild plants,” Conover says. “It helped me see my plant neighbors in a whole new light. And I got to make some tasty treats to share with my family as well.”

Tyrant Lizard Queen is the only work of fiction on our list. But it’s rooted in real science, and stars a Tyrannosaurus rex. Author Riley Black “offers an empathetic look at a real-life creature that experienced hunger and pain, much like the animals that surround us today,” says Science News Explores assistant editor Aaron Tremper, who chose the book as his favorite of 2026. “Black’s penchant for story makes for a thrilling read that fans of Jurassic Park and King Kong can get behind.”

And for those interested in bioethics, we suggest picking up Every Living Creature. Author and physician Joshua D. Mezrich offers a comprehensive look at the field of xenotransplantation, through the stories of courageous doctors and patients who helped make it possible. “At times, the story can feel like a whirlwind, whisking readers across decades and from lab to lab and surgery to surgery,” Rosen wrote in her online review. “But at its core, Every Living Creature is a book about hope.”

A new positioning technology could make autonomous vehicles and robotaxis more reliable at recharging themselves.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Researchers in Japan have developed a new technology that could enable electric vehicles (EVs) to charge "simply by parking".

Wireless charging is still relatively nascent in the EV market, but scientists hope that integrating more wireless charging devices into roads and parking spaces will move the EV industry away from bulky plug-in infrastructure. It uses the same wireless power transfer technology found in modern smartphones and consumer electronics: a transmitter coil inside in a ground pad generates an oscillating magnetic field, which induces an electric current in a receiver coil underneath the vehicle. This current recharges the EV's battery cells.

However, small misalignments between the two coils can affect how quickly and efficiently the battery recharges. This new system uses short-range radio signals to determine the position of the vehicle's magnetic charging coil relative to the charging device in the ground, including its distance and angle. This helps the EV and its driver get into the optimal position for efficient charging.

The technology could be particularly useful for driverless "robotaxis" and other autonomous vehicles that need to be able to recharge quickly and efficiently without human assistance, the researchers said. They detailed their findings in a study published Aug. 26 in the IEEE Open Journal of Vehicular Technology.

"We hope this research will lead to a future where EVs charge simply by parking, much like smartphones placed on wireless chargers," Ryotaro Hada, first author of the study and a master's student at the University of Osaka's Graduate School of Information Science and Technology, said in a statement.

Existing methods for aligning an EV's charging coil with a wireless charging pad use magnetic sensors or cameras. Magnetic systems work best when the coil is close to the pad, while cameras can struggle in rain, poor lighting or when dirt obscures the pad, the researchers explained.

This new system uses four ultra-wideband radio devices mounted around the vehicle's charging coil to communicate with four antennas around the charging pad.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

By measuring how long radio waves take to travel between the ultra-wideband devices and the antennas, as well as detecting tiny differences in how the signals arrive at each of the vehicle's sensors, the system can pinpoint the position and angle of the EV's charging coil relative to the ground pad.

The same technology is used in some digital car keys. They use short radio pulses to detect when the driver is close by, allowing the driver to unlock their vehicle without requiring a physical key.

In laboratory experiments using a scaled-down vehicle model, the system worked out where the vehicle's charging coil was to within 0.09 inches (2.32 millimeters) of its actual position and which direction it was facing to within 0.25 degrees. Correcting for distortions in the radio signals reduced the positioning error by around fivefold, the team said.

The researchers noted that the system still needs to be tested outdoors, on full-size EVs and under real charging conditions.

#6220. New Congress will still be filled with losers

The Capitol Dome is illuminated before dawn on Oct. 13. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

OPINION — Once again, the next Congress is going to be filled with losers.

This is not a personal judgment about their character or personality, but a simple recognition that many members have lost races before getting elected. And the incoming class is no different.

I’ve written many versions of this column for more than a decade, and yet the lesson always seems to get lost, no pun intended. Parties routinely attack candidates who enter a race with losses on their record. And, of course, it happened this cycle as well.

“We beat him once. We’ll beat him again,” National Republican Senatorial Committee Chairman Tim Scott declared when Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown announced his challenge to appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted in the summer of 2025.

“Ohioans gladly sent him packing last year, and they’ll not hesitate to toss him aside again,” said a Republican strategist.

Brown lost reelection to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024 but came back to defeat Husted for the state’s other Senate seat. And Brown is far from the only candidate to avenge a loss with an electoral victory last week.

The fact of the matter is that losing a race doesn’t have to be the end of a political career. Losses can lay the foundation for future success by building name ID or a fundraising network. Or sometimes it takes a change in the political environment or change in circumstances, such as running for an open seat instead of challenging an incumbent.

In addition to Brown, there are more than a dozen losers coming into the next Congress:

In some instances, though, the losses are piling up.

Republican Rep. John James of Michigan now has three statewide losses on his record. He lost Senate contests in 2018 (taking 46 percent of the vote) and 2020 (48 percent) and came up short in his bid for governor this year (44 percent).

Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu of New Hampshire, who lost reelection in 2008 to Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, fell in his comeback attempt for the open seat last week.

But they could take heart from another repeat loser. Charlie Crist, a former Florida governor and congressman, has had a handful of high-profile losses over the years, including for Senate and two gubernatorial comeback bids. He was just elected mayor of St. Petersburg.

So even though I know it’s a futile request, let’s have a bipartisan agreement not to attack candidates for past losses, because losing doesn’t mean they can’t later pull off a win.

#6219. The Secret Reason Why Ancient Roman Concrete Is So Remarkably Strong—And How One Engineer Has Recreated It

He has good reason to believe this marvel of ancient Rome may surpass all modern concrete methods.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

The Pantheon, Rome’s unreinforced concrete dome, constructed around 118 to 125 C.E., still stands intact to this day. The Aqua Virgo, part of the ancient Roman system of aqueducts, was built in 19 B.C.E., yet still supplies Roman fountains, including Trevi, today. Is it any wonder that ancient Rome still draws our global admiration?

For decades, researchers credited the inclusion of volcanic ash from Pozzuoli, a city in Naples, Italy, for the unique strength in the mix; others claimed that lime, a calcium oxide or calcium hydroxide binder created from heating limestone, was the key ingredient. Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Admir Masic, a civil and environmental engineering professor, thought there must be more to the story.

Masic established a lab at MIT with the specific goal of researching ancient Roman concrete. First and foremost a chemist, he says he knew there was something beneath the surface of Roman concrete potentially lending it strength. His team of researchers, from MIT, Harvard, Italy, and Switzerland, discovered that ancient Roman concrete gets its strength—and therefore its incredible longevity—from its inherent self-healing properties. As cracks form, the surrounding material somehow fills them back in, over and over.

Scientists commonly suspected that ash, and not lime, was the hero of the Roman concrete-making process, because the Romans were the first to add volcanic ash to the mixture. This hydration-based method gives the mixture additional strength and makes it possible to build in all seasons.

But it didn’t explain the self-healing quality. Another mystery was in the concrete’s apparent crystalline phases, known to take shape only at high temperatures—at least 80 degrees Celsius (or about 176 degrees Fahrenheit). Yet, the Romans wouldn’t have exposed their concrete mixture to those sorts of temperatures.

Then, researchers discovered calcium aluminate hydrate being used as a binding agent in ancient Roman concrete, which only created further intrigue. This is where the mystery of self-healing gained its first big clue—trying to learn where the calcium came from, Masic says. So his team’s focus shifted to the overlooked role of lime, which is primarily composed of calcium compounds.

Masic notes that modern concrete, when mixed with lime, volcanic components, and water, creates a homogeneous mixture—quite unlike ancient Roman concrete, which is studded with tiny, distinct white particles. “How is it possible that every construction site would make this heterogeneous material even though they put so much effort [into] making it very standard in terms of ingredients [and] how to mix it?” Masic wondered.

The research team decided to investigate the mechanical, structural, and chemical properties of these particles, dubbed “lime clasts,” which were present in every sample they analyzed, Masic says. It led the team to realize “that lime clasts are not an error in mixing, or sloppy mixing, but they are the root of a very specific way of mixing mortars.” Not present in modern concrete, but ubiquitous in the ancient Roman version.

Originally, researchers believed that the Romans added water to the lime mixture to make a slurry. This “slaking” creates a homogeneously structured mixture. However, the presence of the lime clasts didn’t fit into this model.

What the Romans actually did was “hot mixing,” which introduces a novel series of chemical reactions. They ground the stone into tiny pieces of calcium oxide and mixed them with volcanic ash and a dry aggregate. Finally, they added water. “This is where the reaction of calcium oxide with water happens, and the entire mix gets hot, [which] releases energy, and creates hot spots up to 200 to 250 degrees Celsius,” Masic explains.

While lime and the ash formed the basis of the mixture, the constellation of millimeter-scale, mineral particles embedded throughout the mortar turned out to be the secret outcome of the hot mixing process. The key to hot mixing is that it doesn’t dissolve all of the lime clasts. Instead, they get systematically embedded into the concrete mix, creating a reservoir of calcium. When water enters a crack, it can dissolve this calcium. Calcium carbonate can then crystallize inside the crack and help seal it. Voila, self-healing concrete. Masic’s team published their findings in the journal Science Advances.

The team’s own recreation of Roman concrete healed a crack within two weeks. A modern concrete mixture didn’t heal at all, allowing water to flow through the crack. Eventually, water seepage like this destroys the integrity of modern concrete structures.

Roman self-healing concrete allows the mixture to last longer and requires less maintenance and less new material for construction—which also reduces emissions during concrete production. Standard cement production, the solid binder in concrete, accounts for about 8 percent of global CO2 emissions today.

Our world actually has various forms of self-healing concrete, such as bioconcrete, in which bacterial spores activate and produce calcium carbonate to fill in cracks. However, the high costs of modern methods keep the industry from using them widely, says Masic. Meanwhile the ancient Roman method offers “self-healing at an extremely competitive price,” he says.

Now that we know the secret, should we return to making concrete this way?

In fact, Masic co-founded a company in 2021, that uses lessons he has learned from studying ancient Roman concrete. Today, DMAT is creating a concrete additive “that increases the lifespan of concrete structures by 50 percent and reduces CO2 emissions to 40% of traditional concrete,” according to MIT’s Climate Portal. As of August 2026, their material is part of underground water tanks, road barriers, and pavement in Italy and Switzerland. DMAT also plans to expand to U.S. infrastructure projects.

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.
